lesson.l01.title: Question First!
lesson.l01.objective1: Turn a vague business question into a specific, testable analytical brief
lesson.l01.objective2: Test how much your answer depends on choices like time window and entity
lesson.l01.objective3: Defend a decision with real evidence and an honestly calibrated confidence
dialogue.l01_briefing.line1: We need to know - are customers becoming less loyal? Leadership wants an answer by Friday.
dialogue.l01_briefing.line2: Just tell me: loyal or not. Shouldn't take long, right?
dialogue.l01_briefing.line3: Before you touch any data - what does 'less loyal' actually mean here? That question could mean five different things.
dialogue.l01_investigation.line1: Here's what NovaMart Go tracks: signups, purchases, app logins, subscription status - about a year of history.
dialogue.l01_investigation.line2: Notice something? 'Loyal' isn't a column in that data. We have to decide what it means before we can measure it.
dialogue.l01_household_reveal.line1: One thing before you lock that in - some of these customer_ids share a household. Same family, same address, separate accounts.
dialogue.l01_household_reveal.line2: It doesn't show up anywhere in the schema. You'd only catch it by asking.
dialogue.l01_coverage_reveal.line1: Also worth knowing - this table only has identified, logged-in customers. Guest checkout never creates a customer_id, so it never lands here.
dialogue.l01_coverage_reveal.line2: Whatever you report, it's really a statement about identified customers. There aren't rows here to say more than that.
dialogue.l01_twist.line1: Before you send that off, let's line up what you actually found. Same customers, same underlying orders - three honest ways of counting them.
dialogue.l01_twist.line2: Two of these changed only the time window. One changed only who counts as a single customer.
dialogue.l01_twist.line3: Nothing here is a mistake. Look how much the story still moves.
dialogue.l01_window_compute.line1: Here's the real number, computed both ways - same customers, same behavior, only the window changed.
dialogue.l01_entity_compute.line1: Same 30-day window as before - only the entity changed this time.
dialogue.l01_mastery.line1: While you're in there - I've got a side question, if you want it. Not required for the brief.
dialogue.l01_mastery.line2: Households that come back for a second purchase - do they actually spend more than the ones who only ever bought once?
dialogue.l01_debrief.line1: That's the real version of this job. Not 'is loyalty declining' - which definition, over which window, counted which way, and what you're still not sure of.
dialogue.l01_debrief.line2: Whoever picks the definition picks the answer. Next time NovaMart asks you something 'simple,' that's still the first move.
lesson.l01.inspection.prompt: What does one row in this table actually represent?
lesson.l01.inspection.hint: There's no wrong pick to worry about here - just look at the columns and decide what one row is really counting.
lesson.l01.grain.title: Grain in Action
lesson.l01.grain.request.order_count.pro: How many orders has each customer actually placed?
lesson.l01.grain.request.order_count.hin: Group by customer and the row count changes completely - same table, different meaning per row.
lesson.l01.grain.request.total_spend.pro: How much has each customer spent in total?
lesson.l01.grain.request.total_spend.hin: Same grouping, a different real number - grain changes what each row can honestly tell you, not just how many there are.
lesson.l01.field.entity.prompt: Who or what are we actually measuring?
lesson.l01.field.entity.hint_tier1: Think about what you'd point to and call 'one.'
lesson.l01.field.entity.hint_tier2: A customer, an account, and a household aren't always the same thing - people can share one and still differ on another.
lesson.l01.field.entity.hint_tier3: You already saw this in the raw data: some customer_ids share a household_id. Pick whichever one your decision actually needs.
lesson.l01.field.time_horizon.hint_tier1: Think about how recent the answer needs to feel.
lesson.l01.field.time_horizon.hint_tier2: A short window reacts fast but is noisier. A long window is stable but can hide a recent shift.
lesson.l01.field.time_horizon.hint_tier3: You'll get to test this directly in a few minutes - for now, pick the window that matches what the PM is actually asking.
lesson.l01.field.behavior.hint: Different behaviors tell different stories - a login isn't the same commitment as a renewal.
lesson.l01.field.population.prompt: Which customers should even be included?
lesson.l01.field.population.hint: Including customers who couldn't possibly show the behavior yet - like brand-new signups - can quietly bias the result.
lesson.l01.option.population.active_last: Only customers active in the last year
lesson.l01.field.metric.prompt: How do we turn that into one number?
lesson.l01.field.metric.hint_tier1: Think about what 'went up' or 'went down' would even mean here.
lesson.l01.field.metric.hint_tier2: A rate, a count, and a median answer slightly different questions, even from the same data.
lesson.l01.field.metric.hint_tier3: Retention rate and churn rate are mirror images of each other - the real choice is usually between a rate and a raw frequency.
lesson.l01.field.decision_support.prompt: What decision should this number actually inform?
lesson.l01.field.decision_support.hint: A brief that isn't tied to a real decision is just trivia - this is what keeps the analysis useful.
lesson.l01.option.decision_support.loyal: Whether to launch a loyalty program
lesson.l01.option.decision_support.escal: Whether to escalate this to leadership as urgent
lesson.l01.window_predict.title: Before You Look
lesson.l01.window_predict.prompt: Guess first: will the last-30-days repeat rate be higher, lower, or about the same as the 12-month rate?
lesson.l01.window_confidence_before.prom: How confident are you in that guess?
lesson.l01.window_confidence_before.hint: Answer honestly - there's no real data behind this guess yet, and that's exactly the point.
lesson.l01.window_compute.title: Same Customers, Two Windows
lesson.l01.window_interpret.prompt: What does this gap actually mean?
lesson.l01.window_interpret.option.real_: A real difference - the window changes the story
lesson.l01.window_interpret.option.needs: Interesting, but I'd want more comparisons first
lesson.l01.entity_revision.title: One More Look
lesson.l01.entity_revision.prompt: Knowing that now - which entity should this actually count?
lesson.l01.entity_revision.hint: Neither answer is automatically wrong - the question is which one your original brief actually needs.
lesson.l01.entity_compute.title: Same Window, Two Entities
lesson.l01.entity_interpret.prompt: What does this shift tell you?
lesson.l01.entity_interpret.option.entit: Entity choice changes the real number
A small difference, not worth worrying about
lesson.l01.coverage_interpret.title: One Thing This Data Can't Do
lesson.l01.coverage_interpret.prompt: Given that, what's the honest thing to do with your claim?
lesson.l01.coverage_interpret.option.nar: Scope the claim to identified customers only
lesson.l01.coverage_interpret.option.num: Treat every number as wrong for now
lesson.l01.decision.claim.prompt: Which of these is the strongest claim you could actually defend?
lesson.l01.decision.claim.option.overrea: Loyalty is declining - full stop, across the board.
lesson.l01.decision.claim.option.well_sc: Repeat-purchase rate is down over 30 days.
lesson.l01.decision.claim.option.either_: It depends entirely on which window you use.
lesson.l01.decision.claim.option.cannot_: Not enough here to say anything meaningful.
lesson.l01.decision.evidence.prompt: Pick 2-3 findings that actually support that claim.
lesson.l01.decision.limitation.prompt: What does your claim not capture?
lesson.l01.decision.limitation.option.de: Depends on the window and entity chosen
lesson.l01.decision.limitation.option.no: It doesn't account for seasonal patterns
Honestly, none - the number speaks for itself
lesson.l01.decision.confidence.prompt: How confident are you in this claim?
lesson.l01.decision.recommendation.promp: What should NovaMart actually do with this?
lesson.l01.decision.follow_up.prompt: What's the one thing worth checking next?
lesson.l01.decision.follow_up.option.get: Get identity data linking guests to customers
lesson.l01.decision.follow_up.option.rer: Re-run the same definition next month
lesson.l01.decision.follow_up.option.not: Nothing further - this is enough to act on
lesson.l01.mastery.title: One More Question, If You Want It
lesson.l01.mastery.interpret_prompt: What does this comparison actually show?
lesson.l01.mastery.interpret_about_same: Not a large enough gap to act on
lesson.l01.feedback.claim_matches_eviden: Your final claim matches what your evidence actually supports.
lesson.l01.feedback.claim_overreaches: Your claim goes further than the evidence and limitation you recorded support.
lesson.l01.feedback.evidence_spans_inves: Your claim draws on evidence from across the investigation, not just the first number you saw.
lesson.l01.feedback.limitation_matches_c: The limitation you named is a real, specific gap in the number you're reporting.
lesson.l01.feedback.confidence_well_cali: Your stated confidence matches how well-supported and well-scoped your claim actually is.
lesson.l01.feedback.mastery_completed: You took on the bonus question too - that's real initiative.

lesson.l02.title: Source Scout
lesson.l02.objective1: Inspect and compare four candidate data sources for one business question
lesson.l02.objective2: Recognize that a source can be right for one part of a question and wrong for another
lesson.l02.objective3: State a defensible answer and name exactly what it does not let you claim
dialogue.l02_briefing.line1: We need a number for the board deck: how many active NovaMart Plus members do we actually have?
dialogue.l02_briefing.line2: Finance wants a defensible figure by Friday. Separately, Product wants to know if it's safe to retire web-only account management and push everyone onto the Go app.
dialogue.l02_briefing.line3: Both of those depend on getting this right, so don't just grab whatever's fastest to pull.
dialogue.l02_framing.line1: There's no single 'active members' table. Four different systems each think they know the answer.
dialogue.l02_framing.line2: Before we compute anything, let's see what we've actually got.
lesson.l02.source_map.title: The Source Map
lesson.l02.source_map.prompt: Four systems, four different views of the same customers. Which would you inspect first?
lesson.l02.source_map.hint: This is a starting point, not a verdict - you'll investigate all four either way.
lesson.l02.source.billing.name: Billing
lesson.l02.source.app_log.name: App Log
lesson.l02.source.marketing.name: Marketing
lesson.l02.source.support.name: Support
lesson.l02.fact.billing.documented_purpo: Track each customer's current billing status
lesson.l02.fact.app_log.documented_purpo: Track when customers use the Go app
lesson.l02.fact.marketing.documented_pur: Track marketing enrollment and trial signups
lesson.l02.fact.support.documented_purpo: Log customer contacts about billing or account issues
lesson.l02.fact.support.freshness: Ad hoc - whenever a case is logged
lesson.l02.billing_inspect.prompt: This table has a status column. What does it actually tell you?
lesson.l02.billing_inspect.hint: Look at what values the column actually holds before assuming what it covers.
lesson.l02.billing_compute.title: Compute Billing's Number
lesson.l02.billing_compute.prompt: Group the table to see how many customers are in each status.
lesson.l02.billing_compute.hint: Grouping by an ID that's unique per row won't tell you anything about status.
lesson.l02.app_log_inspect.prompt: Who is even in this table in the first place?
lesson.l02.app_log_inspect.hint: Check whether every Plus member you know from Billing also shows up here.
lesson.l02.app_log_inspect.option.app_us: Only customers who use the Go app
lesson.l02.comparison1.title: First Conflict: Billing vs. the App Log
dialogue.l02_comparison1.line1: Billing says 100 members are actively paying.
dialogue.l02_comparison1.line2: The Go app's own activity log says 95 were active in the last 30 days.
dialogue.l02_comparison1.line3: Both calculations can be correct under their own definitions; they answer different questions.
One of these two numbers must be wrong
lesson.l02.marketing_inspect.prompt: Who does this list actually include?
lesson.l02.marketing_inspect.hint: Check whether it only covers people currently paying, or something broader.
lesson.l02.marketing_inspect.option.only: Only customers active in the app
lesson.l02.comparison2.title: Second Conflict: Billing vs. Marketing
dialogue.l02_comparison2.line2: Marketing's CRM export says 168 enrolled - trial signups included, never billed.
lesson.l02.comparison2_interpret.prompt: What best explains this much bigger gap?
Marketing's number must be inflated by mistake
lesson.l02.gap.title: Naming the Gap
dialogue.l02_gap.line1: Marketing's list covers every customer NovaMart has ever billed or enrolled. Billing's table doesn't.
dialogue.l02_gap.line2: 38 customers show up in Marketing with zero rows in Billing at all.
lesson.l02.gap_interpret.prompt: What's the best read on that missing 38?
lesson.l02.gap_interpret.option.all_a_bu: All 38 are a data pipeline bug
lesson.l02.gap_interpret.option.mixed_an: A mix: 30 genuinely missing, status unknown
dialogue.l02_finance_lead.line1: That gap's real, and I know exactly where it's from - we switched payment processors a few months back.
dialogue.l02_finance_lead.line2: The 30 accounts missing from Billing are still on the old processor. Nobody's re-synced their current status since.
lesson.l02.revision.title: Given What You Know Now
lesson.l02.revision.prompt: Would you still rely on Billing alone?
lesson.l02.revision.hint: No penalty either way - this is just a checkpoint on where you actually stand.
lesson.l02.revision.option.still_billing: Yes, Billing alone is still fine
lesson.l02.revision.option.billing_plus_: No, it needs to be combined with something
lesson.l02.support.title: One More List: Support's Spreadsheet
dialogue.l02_support.line1: Customer Success keeps its own list of high-touch accounts - 22 rows, hand-maintained.
dialogue.l02_support.line2: Two of those rows are the same customer, pasted in twice by accident.
lesson.l02.support_interpret.prompt: What does the gap between raw rows and unique customers tell you?
lesson.l02.support_interpret.option.dedu: Check for duplicate IDs before trusting the count
lesson.l02.support_interpret.option.dupl: 2 duplicates out of 22 is close enough to ignore
lesson.l02.support_interpret.option.list: The duplicates make this whole list worthless
lesson.l02.decision.answer_strategy.prom: How should this actually be reported?
lesson.l02.decision.answer_strategy.opti: 100 confirmed active - the missing 30 don't count
No usable answer without a whole new data pull
lesson.l02.decision.known_gap.prompt: What's the specific gap in this data?
lesson.l02.decision.known_gap.option.leg: Billing excludes accounts on the old processor
lesson.l02.decision.known_gap.option.tra: The app log's activity tracking has a bug
lesson.l02.decision.known_gap.option.gen: The data might not be fully accurate
lesson.l02.decision.known_gap.option.no_: No gap left once you combine the sources
lesson.l02.decision.safe_to_claim.prompt: What is this safe to claim?
lesson.l02.decision.safe_to_claim.option: A confirmed floor and range for a board estimate
The exact active count, down to the individual
lesson.l02.decision.not_safe_to_claim.pr: What is this NOT safe to claim?
lesson.l02.decision.not_safe_to_claim.op: A single exact total, whatever the number
Precise enough for individual access decisions
The range itself is also unsafe to use
lesson.l02.decision.recommendation.optio: Report the range; reconcile status separately
Block the board deck until the data is perfect
lesson.l02.evidence.app_log_active_label: App log, active in last 30 days:
lesson.l02.evidence.legacy_status_unreso: No source confirms the missing accounts' status
lesson.l02.mastery.title: One More Question, If You're Up For It
dialogue.l02_mastery.line1: Finance's own analyst has a follow-up: is Support's list a fair sample of how common these old-processor accounts are?
dialogue.l02_mastery.line2: Same four sources - a genuinely different question.
lesson.l02.mastery.metric_prompt: How should you compare Support's list to the full customer base?
lesson.l02.mastery.interpret_prompt: What does the comparison tell you?
lesson.l02.mastery.interpret_raw_already: The raw counts already answer this
lesson.l02.mastery.support_share_label: Support list's own share, old processor:
lesson.l02.mastery.population_share_labe: Full customer base's share, old processor:
lesson.l02.feedback.honest_floor_and_ran: Your answer reports a confirmed floor and an honest range, not a single number pretending to be more certain than it is.
lesson.l02.feedback.answer_mishandles_th: Your answer treats an unresolved population as if its status were already known.
lesson.l02.feedback.evidence_covers_the_: Your evidence covers what actually matters: the confirmed count, the gap, and that it's still unresolved.
lesson.l02.feedback.gap_named_precisely: You named the specific gap, not a generic caveat.
lesson.l02.feedback.scope_is_coherent: What you called safe and unsafe actually line up with each other and with what you found.
lesson.l02.feedback.scope_contradicts_it: What you called safe and unsafe contradict each other.
lesson.l02.feedback.revised_after_new_ev: You started by trusting Billing, then genuinely revised that once the gap came to light - that's the whole point.
lesson.l02.feedback.mastery_completed: You took on the bonus question too - that shows initiative.
dialogue.l02_debrief.line1: The skill here wasn't picking a source. It was noticing which question each one could actually answer.
dialogue.l02_debrief.line2: 'Official' isn't the same as 'right for this question.' Ask what a number leaves out before you ship it.

lesson.l03.title: API Courier
lesson.l03.objective1: Pull data through a paginated API instead of assuming one request gets everything
lesson.l03.objective2: Notice that a successful status code doesn't guarantee a complete response
lesson.l03.objective3: Judge whether an acquired dataset is complete enough to analyze
dialogue.l03_briefing.line1: Support flagged what looks like a spike in cancellation events last week - before we escalate to Engineering, I need a real count.
dialogue.l03_briefing.line2: Policy escalates any week with 130 or more cancellation events. Below that, it's normal noise.
dialogue.l03_briefing.line3: I need this for a decision today, not next week - pull what the API gives you and tell me where we stand.
dialogue.l03_framing.line1: The endpoint paginates - 25 records a page. Fetch, read the response, decide whether to fetch again.
dialogue.l03_framing.line2: Watch every response's status and what it actually contains - a page can come back fine and still short you.
dialogue.l03_completeness_reveal.line1: You pulled every page the API offered - but "every page responded" isn't the same as "every page delivered."
dialogue.l03_completeness_reveal.line2: Compare what you actually collected against what the API itself says should be there.
dialogue.l03_root_cause.line1: I checked page 3 on our end.
dialogue.l03_root_cause.line2: It hit a transient fault on that shard - the response still came back 200 OK, still said more pages followed, it just quietly shipped short. Nine records never left our servers.
dialogue.l03_mastery.line1: One more thing, if you've got time: Support wants a count from their own ticket feed too.
dialogue.l03_mastery.line2: Same endpoint shape, smaller pull. See if the same instinct holds up.
dialogue.l03_debrief.line1: The 429 was visible and recoverable - the status said exactly what was wrong.
dialogue.l03_debrief.line2: Page 3 was the more dangerous one. It never told you anything was wrong at all.
lesson.l03.console_hint: Read has_more before deciding whether to fetch again - and check the record count even when the status says OK.
lesson.l03.gut_check.title: Quick Check
lesson.l03.gut_check.prompt: Based on what you just pulled, do you think you got everything?
lesson.l03.gut_check.hint: There's no wrong answer here - this is just a checkpoint, not a grade.
lesson.l03.completeness_reveal.title: What You Actually Got
lesson.l03.completeness_interpret.option: A page silently returned fewer records
The rate limit alone fully explains it
The naturally smaller last page explains it
The API's declared total must be wrong
lesson.l03.revised_gut_check.title: Second Look
lesson.l03.revised_gut_check.prompt: Given what you know now, would you still report the raw number as-is?
lesson.l03.decision.acquisition_strategy: Report the raw total as final, no caveat
A floor, a named shortfall, a flagged threshold
Refuse to report until a full re-pull
Discard the whole pull and start over
lesson.l03.decision.known_gap.prompt: What's the specific gap in this data?
lesson.l03.decision.known_gap.option.pag: A page silently returned fewer records
A short page, and a second page lost entirely
lesson.l03.decision.known_gap.option.rat: The rate limit alone fully explains the gap
lesson.l03.decision.known_gap.option.not: What was received accounts for everything
lesson.l03.decision.known_gap.option.pag: The API's pagination is fundamentally broken
lesson.l03.decision.safe_to_claim.option: A confirmed floor; may still cross the threshold
The exact true count, precise to the record
That the gap is too small to matter here
lesson.l03.decision.not_safe_to_claim.op: That the API is unreliable for any future pull
That even the floor and range can't be trusted
lesson.l03.decision.recommendation.optio: Report the range, escalate, and flag the fault
Report the raw total and move on
Block the decision on a full re-pull
lesson.l03.mastery.title: One More Pull, If You're Up For It
lesson.l03.mastery.metric_prompt: How do you want to check this one?
lesson.l03.mastery.metric_last_page_vs_p: Compare the last page against a full page
lesson.l03.mastery.metric_received_vs_de: Compare received vs. the declared total
lesson.l03.mastery.interpret_last_page_s: The last page is short of what the API declares
lesson.l03.mastery.interpret_looks_compl: Nothing to flag - a small last page is normal
lesson.l03.feedback.floor_and_range: Your answer reports a confirmed floor and an honest range, not a single number pretending to be more certain than it is.
lesson.l03.feedback.recovered_via_backof: You recovered the rate-limited page instead of leaving a real hole in the data - that's the retry discipline this lesson is about.
lesson.l03.feedback.evidence_covers_the_: Your evidence covers what actually matters: the confirmed floor, the declared total, and the real mechanism behind the gap.
lesson.l03.feedback.gap_named_precisely: You named the specific mechanism behind the gap, not a generic caveat.
lesson.l03.feedback.scope_is_coherent: What's safe and not safe to claim actually line up with each other and with what the data supports.
lesson.l03.feedback.scope_contradicts_it: Calling the confirmed floor and range both safe and untrustworthy at once doesn't hold together.
lesson.l03.feedback.revised_after_the_re: You assumed the pull was complete, then correctly flagged it once the reveal showed the real gap - that's the whole point.
lesson.l03.feedback.mastery_solved: You took on the bonus question and got it right - that's the transfer this was testing for.
lesson.l03.feedback.mastery_attempted: You took on the bonus question - the read was off this time, but engaging with it is what counts.
dialogue.l04_briefing.line1: NovaMart Go's new checkout ships Thursday - I need the event tracking plan signed off before it goes live.
dialogue.l04_briefing.line2: I need to know where people drop off between viewing their cart and confirming an order.
dialogue.l04_briefing.line3: Support's already asked me something specific: if a customer says they were charged twice, can we confirm that from the logs?
dialogue.l04_briefing.line4: And Growth wants to separate people who abandon at payment from people whose payment actually gets declined.
dialogue.l04_briefing.line5: A launch is the only time you get to plan tracking before the data exists. Miss a step now, and that data is just gone.
dialogue.l04_briefing.line6: Let's design the spec together first.
dialogue.l04_framing.line1: Most of the funnel's already instrumented and stable - page views, add to cart, all of that ships as-is.
dialogue.l04_framing.line2: Two events actually need real design work for this launch: order_confirmed needs a cleaner trigger, and payment_attempted is brand new.
dialogue.l04_framing.line3: For each one: exactly when it should fire, what identifiers it carries, and what properties we'll actually need later.
dialogue.l04_event_a_reveal.line1: Here's what actually got logged after a week of real checkout sessions.
dialogue.l04_event_a_reveal.line2: Compare the raw log against what you'd expect if every order confirmed exactly once.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_clean.line1: order_confirmed only fires once the gateway itself confirms the charge, and every row carries a real order_id.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_clean.line2: That's exactly why we always confirm from the server side - a client-side trigger can't tell a slow response from a failed one.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_trigger.line1: Found it: order_confirmed fires the moment the client sees a response, and a slow gateway response gets retried.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_trigger.line2: Look at the timestamps on a duplicate pair - about two to three seconds apart. That's a retry, not two separate orders.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_identifiers.line: The trigger's fine, but order_confirmed never carries order_id - only session_id.
Without order_id, we can count sessions, but we can't confirm which specific order a customer is asking about.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_both.line1: Found two real problems, not one: order_confirmed fires client-side, and it never carries order_id.
dialogue.l04_root_cause_both.line2: Without order_id we can't even try to dedupe - both need fixing before this ships.
dialogue.l04_mastery.line1: One more flow, no hints this time: the new account signup just shipped its own account_created event.
dialogue.l04_mastery.line2: Same kind of question - does the raw count tell the real story?
dialogue.l04_debrief.line1: A tracking plan isn't done when the events exist - it's done when it can answer the questions people will actually ask.
dialogue.l04_debrief.line2: The trigger you pick isn't a technicality. It's the difference between one order and two on somebody's bill.
lesson.l04.title: Event Log Factory
lesson.l04.objective1: Design an event's real trigger, identifiers, and properties - not just its name
lesson.l04.objective2: Discover what a tracking design actually produces by simulating real sessions against it

dialogue.l05_briefing.line1: Partner renegotiation call is in three weeks. I need a number I can defend: what share of deliveries actually had a problem last quarter.
dialogue.l05_briefing.line2: A full audit of every delivery isn't happening - we've got budget for 80, out of roughly a thousand.
dialogue.l05_briefing.line3: Support's complaint list is already sitting there, if you want the fast read.
dialogue.l05_framing.line1: Before you pick anything: the population is every delivery that happened. A frame is whatever list you can actually draw from - and those aren't automatically the same thing.
dialogue.l05_framing.line2: Three lists exist: the fulfillment tracking export, this month's support tickets, and the loyalty app's delivery ratings.
dialogue.l05_framing.line3: None of them is the full population. Which one you draw from - and how - is the whole job.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_tickets.line1: A support ticket only exists because someone had a problem worth complaining about. Nobody files one to say a delivery was fine.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_tickets.line2: So this list isn't a slice of all deliveries - it's a list of complaints, and it'll look like almost everything failed.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_loyalty.line1: The loyalty app skews the other way: it's mostly used by Metro customers, and by people who liked their delivery enough to bother rating it.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_loyalty.line2: A rough delivery is exactly the kind of thing that makes someone skip the app and go straight to support instead.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_coverage.line1: The tracking export is our best list - but QuickShip's Rural deliveries sync in through a separate manual log, and most of this quarter's batch hasn't landed yet.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_coverage.line2: Rural is the one region with a real problem rate worth worrying about, and it's the one this list barely sees.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_order.line1: The export lists deliveries in the order they were entered - and the first 80 rows in that order happen to all be Metro.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_order.line2: Nothing about that was self-selected. It's just what sat at the top of an unsorted list.
dialogue.l05_root_cause_pivot.line1: Let's also see what a plain random draw from the fullest list looks like, so you've got something real to compare against.
dialogue.l05_reveal1.line1: Here's what your pick actually produced, drawn for real from the hidden population.
dialogue.l05_reveal1.line2: Look at how much of it is Rural before you trust the headline number.
dialogue.l05_reveal2.line1: Same question, but drawn plainly at random from the fullest available list.
dialogue.l05_reveal2.line2: See how the picture changes once the frame itself is the best one available.
dialogue.l05_reveal3.line1: One more honest draw - same design, same frame, a different random pull.
dialogue.l05_reveal3.line2: Nobody did anything differently this time. Compare the two numbers anyway.
dialogue.l05_reveal4.line1: Here's what your second design actually produced.
dialogue.l05_reveal4.line2: Check whether Rural's own share moved compared to the plain random draws.
dialogue.l05_debrief.line1: A random sample is only as good as the list it was drawn from. Before you trust any number, ask one thing: random - but random from what?
dialogue.l05_debrief.line2: That question is the whole lesson. Frame first, method second - never the other way around.
dialogue.l05_debrief.line3: So which number actually goes in front of the partner - and which regions can I not claim it covers?
dialogue.l05_mastery.line1: One more question before you go: what's the problem rate specifically for Express deliveries?
dialogue.l05_mastery.line2: You already have a sample - but it was never designed with Express in mind. See what it actually gives you.

dialogue.l07_briefing.line3: Missing isn't always random. Worth checking where it's missing before deciding how to fill it.
dialogue.l07_briefing.line4: Let's compare a few honest approaches before picking one.
dialogue.l07_investigation.line1: Five ways to handle it are laid out side by side - each shows its own resulting average, sample size, and how it actually treats the missing rows.
dialogue.l07_investigation.line2: The headline number isn't the whole story. Read the sample size and handling notes too.
dialogue.l07_investigation.line3: Pick the one you'd actually put in front of the board.
dialogue.l07_independent_intro.line1: Good instinct. Compare the same five again on your own - no hints this time.
dialogue.l07_twist.line1: Every strategy above only used what was actually recorded - nobody had the customers who never responded.
dialogue.l07_twist.line2: Here's what NovaMart eventually learned once follow-up calls filled in the real numbers.
dialogue.l07_debrief.line1: The customers with no score weren't random - they were the most disengaged of the at-risk group. Every unweighted approach overstated things.
dialogue.l07_debrief.line2: Segment-aware imputation got closest - not because it's fancy, but because it's the only approach that used what we already knew about who was missing.
dialogue.l07_debrief.line3: 'Closest' isn't 'correct', though. It still leaned on the at-risk customers who did respond, and they might not represent the ones who didn't.
lesson.l07.title: Missing Data Clinic
lesson.l07.objective1: Compare how different missing-data strategies change a reported average
lesson.l07.objective2: Recognize when missingness is correlated with a customer segment, not random
lesson.l07.objective3: Choose a strategy and name the bias that remains even after it
lesson.l07.board_prompt: Compare how each strategy treats the missing engagement scores.
lesson.l07.board_hint: Two strategies can show the same headline number for very different reasons - check the sample size too.
lesson.l07.twist_true_label: True average (every customer had a score):
lesson.l07.field.strategy_choice.prompt: Which approach is worth presenting to the board?
lesson.l07.field.strategy_choice.hint: The closest-to-truth option isn't always the simplest one to explain.
lesson.l07.option.strategy_choice.segmen: Segment-aware fill - closest to the truth
lesson.l07.option.strategy_choice.preser: Preserve missingness and report it separately
lesson.l07.option.strategy_choice.drop_r: Drop incomplete rows - simplest, overstates it
lesson.l07.field.remaining_bias.prompt: Even with the best approach, what bias remains?
lesson.l07.field.remaining_bias.hint: Name a specific gap, not just that the data is 'incomplete'.
lesson.l07.option.remaining_bias.respond: Who responded may not represent who did not
lesson.l07.option.remaining_bias.no_data: Customers with no history are missing too
dialogue.l08_briefing.line1: Customer records from three different systems need to be unified before the CRM migration next week.
dialogue.l08_briefing.line2: Just merge whatever looks like the same person - I don't want three profiles for one customer.
dialogue.l08_briefing.line3: Merging is easy. Un-merging two real people you accidentally combined is not - let's actually look at each case.
dialogue.l08_briefing.line4: Same name, same phone, same address - none of those alone proves it's the same person. Let's see what the records actually show.
dialogue.l08_investigation.line1: Five candidate pairs are flagged, one at a time. Differing fields are highlighted.
dialogue.l08_investigation.line2: A matching name or phone isn't automatically a duplicate - families share addresses and phones too.
dialogue.l08_investigation.line3: Decide Merge or Keep Separate for each, based on what's actually in front of you.
dialogue.l08_independent_intro.line1: Good eye. Review the same five again on your own - no hints this time.
dialogue.l08_twist.line1: Every pair you reviewed got individual attention - most automated matching doesn't.
dialogue.l08_twist.line2: Here's what happened when a stricter rule and a looser rule both ran across NovaMart's full backlog of flagged pairs.
dialogue.l08_debrief.line1: The aggressive rule caught every real duplicate - and merged 10 real, distinct people into someone else's record.
dialogue.l08_debrief.line2: The conservative rule never merged the wrong person - but missed 6 real duplicates that only shared one signal.
dialogue.l08_debrief.line3: Neither number is 'the' answer. Which mistake costs more is a business question, not a technical one.
lesson.l08.title: Duplicate Detective
lesson.l08.objective1: Tell a real duplicate from a coincidental match using multiple fields, not one
lesson.l08.objective2: Compare an aggressive and a conservative matching rule at scale
lesson.l08.objective3: Choose a matching rule and explain the precision/recall trade-off behind it
lesson.l08.board_prompt: Compare the two records. Highlighted fields differ.
lesson.l08.twist_title: Two Rules, Two Kinds of Mistakes
lesson.l08.pair.spelling_and_casing.hint: A nickname and inconsistent capitalization aren't the same as different information.
lesson.l08.pair.changed_address.hint: People move. An old address doesn't outweigh three exact matches.
lesson.l08.pair.shared_phone.hint: A shared phone or address often means the same household, not the same person.
lesson.l08.pair.duplicate_signup.hint: When every field matches exactly, this is usually just one person with two accounts.
lesson.l08.pair.name_coincidence.hint: A shared name alone is common. Look at everything else before deciding.
lesson.l08.field.name: Name
lesson.l08.field.matching_rule_choice.pr: Which matching rule should NovaMart actually use?
lesson.l08.field.matching_rule_choice.hi: There's no rule with zero mistakes - only different kinds of them.
lesson.l08.option.matching_rule_choice.c: Conservative - require multiple signals to agree
lesson.l08.option.matching_rule_choice.a: Aggressive - merge on any strong signal
lesson.l08.option.matching_rule_choice.c: Conservative, plus flag near-misses for review
lesson.l08.field.tradeoff_reasoning.prom: What's the real cost of getting this wrong?
lesson.l08.field.tradeoff_reasoning.hint: Name which mistake is worse here, not just that mistakes happen.
lesson.l08.option.tradeoff_reasoning.fal: A wrong merge combines two people's data
lesson.l08.option.tradeoff_reasoning.mis: A missed duplicate is just a redundant record
lesson.l08.option.tradeoff_reasoning.asy: The two mistakes are not equally costly
dialogue.l09_briefing.line1: NovaPay's fraud model keeps flagging huge transactions - I just want one number: are we losing money or not?
dialogue.l09_briefing.line2: Whatever's over $20,000, we've been excluding it automatically. Feels safe. Tell me it's working.
dialogue.l09_briefing.line3: It's not that simple - 'extreme' doesn't mean the same kind of extreme every time.
dialogue.l09_briefing.line4: Let's look at a few of these cases individually before trusting one number - or one rule - for all of them.
dialogue.l09_investigation.line1: Five outlier transactions, one at a time. Each has its own context - customer history, timing, amount.
dialogue.l09_investigation.line2: The options aren't always the same three - pick whichever actually fits what you're looking at.
dialogue.l09_investigation.line3: 'Extreme' can mean fraud, a data error, or just a big legitimate order. Read the context first.
dialogue.l09_independent_intro.line1: Good instincts. Review five more on your own - no hints this time.
dialogue.l09_twist.line1: The $20,000 blanket rule has been running for months, quietly excluding everything above it.
dialogue.l09_twist.line2: Here's what those 20 excluded transactions actually turned out to be.
dialogue.l09_debrief.line1: Only a quarter were fraud. Most were real enterprise orders the rule couldn't tell apart from a threat.
dialogue.l09_debrief.line2: So we've been turning away legitimate revenue this whole time.
dialogue.l09_debrief.line3: One rule, applied everywhere, always misses this - some of these cases needed a person to actually look, not a threshold.
lesson.l09.title: Outlier Patrol
lesson.l09.objective1: Judge extreme values by context, not by size alone
lesson.l09.objective2: Pick the right action from several - retain, flag, exclude, cap, or investigate
lesson.l09.objective3: Explain why one global rule can't correctly handle every kind of outlier
lesson.l09.board_title: What Should Happen to This Transaction?
lesson.l09.twist_title: What the Blanket Rule Actually Caught
lesson.l09.case.consistent_enterprise_or: $48,000 from Meridian Logistics, a returning customer whose last 6 orders ranged $40,000-$55,000. What should happen to this transaction?
A large amount that matches the customer's own history isn't an anomaly.
lesson.l09.case.new_account_spike.label: New Account Spike
lesson.l09.case.new_account_spike.prompt: $12,000 from an account opened 3 weeks ago, whose every prior order was under $800. What should happen to this transaction?
lesson.l09.case.new_account_spike.hint: Unusual isn't the same as fraudulent - but it's not nothing either.
lesson.l09.case.test_artifact.label: Test Artifact
lesson.l09.case.test_artifact.prompt: A $0.00 entry logged outside business hours during a payment-system test window, with no linked order ID. What should happen to this transaction?
lesson.l09.case.test_artifact.hint: This isn't a real economic event at all - it shouldn't be analyzed as one.
lesson.l09.case.decimal_slip.label: Decimal Slip
lesson.l09.case.decimal_slip.prompt: $2,500,000 from a customer whose typical order is $2,500 - the amount matches exactly, times 1,000. What should happen to this transaction?
lesson.l09.case.decimal_slip.hint: The underlying order is probably real. The value just needs correcting, not discarding.
lesson.l09.case.fraud_signals.label: Fraud Signals
lesson.l09.case.fraud_signals.prompt: $30,000 shipped to a new address in a different country, made minutes after three failed card attempts on the same account. What should happen to this transaction?
lesson.l09.case.fraud_signals.hint: This matches real fraud patterns - but a closer look, not an instant verdict, is the right first move.
lesson.l09.field.rule_approach.prompt: What should replace the flat $20,000 cutoff?
lesson.l09.field.rule_approach.hint: The cases you just reviewed didn't share one correct action - the process shouldn't assume they will either.
lesson.l09.option.rule_approach.context_: Route extreme values to context-aware review
lesson.l09.option.rule_approach.raise_th: Just raise the threshold - keep it simple
lesson.l09.option.rule_approach.keep_rul: Keep the rule, but flag instead of excluding
lesson.l09.field.remaining_limitation.pr: What would still need attention even with a better process?
lesson.l09.field.remaining_limitation.hi: Name a cost the fix itself introduces, not just the old rule's mistake.
lesson.l09.option.remaining_limitation.r: Manual review doesn't scale up easily
lesson.l09.option.remaining_limitation.c: The three categories can look identical
lesson.l09.option.remaining_limitation.d: Holding transactions for review has its own cost
dialogue.l10_briefing.line1: The new daily orders feed needs to be validated before analytics can touch it - can you set up the checks?
dialogue.l10_briefing.line2: I don't need every possible check - just enough that we can trust this specific analysis.
dialogue.l10_briefing.line3: There are six standard checks worth knowing. Each one needs calibrating to this feed, not applied blindly.
dialogue.l10_briefing.line4: A check that's too strict blocks good data. Too loose, and it misses real problems. Let's get each one right.
dialogue.l10_investigation.line1: Six checks, one at a time - uniqueness, ranges, nulls, references, freshness, categories.
dialogue.l10_investigation.line2: For each one, you'll see what this feed actually looks like. Pick the rule that fits it.
dialogue.l10_investigation.line3: Once the suite passes, that doesn't mean the data is right - it means it cleared the bar you set.
dialogue.l10_independent_intro.line1: Good calibration. Build the same suite again, on your own - no hints this time.
dialogue.l10_twist.line1: Your validation suite passed this feed clean - every one of the six checks.
dialogue.l10_twist.line2: Here's what a closer look at the actual order amounts found.
dialogue.l10_debrief.line1: Fifty orders were recorded in cents, not dollars - and every one of them still looked like a plausible order amount.
dialogue.l10_debrief.line2: None of the six checks were built to catch that - they check structure, not meaning.
dialogue.l10_debrief.line3: A dataset can be perfectly well-formed and still say something untrue.
lesson.l10.title: Validation Gate
lesson.l10.objective1: Calibrate a validation check to what a specific feed actually looks like
lesson.l10.objective2: Recognize that passing checks confirms structure, not correctness
lesson.l10.objective3: Design a validation suite sufficient for a specific analysis, not a generic checklist
lesson.l10.board_title: What Rule Should This Check Use?
lesson.l10.check.uniqueness.label: Uniqueness
lesson.l10.check.uniqueness.prompt: 10,000 order_id values in the feed. What should the uniqueness check do?
lesson.l10.check.uniqueness.hint: A duplicate order_id means something downstream will double-count.
lesson.l10.check.allowed_range.label: Allowed Range
lesson.l10.check.allowed_range.prompt: Order amounts have ranged from $5 to $48,000 in past feeds, including known large enterprise orders. What range should this check accept?
lesson.l10.check.allowed_range.hint: Enterprise orders can legitimately be large - don't design a range that rejects real business.
lesson.l10.rule.allowed_range.no_check: Skip it - amounts don't need a range
lesson.l10.check.null_limit.label: Null Limit
lesson.l10.check.null_limit.prompt: 2% of rows are missing a customer email, all from one known legacy import batch. What should the null check allow?
lesson.l10.check.null_limit.hint: Zero tolerance would fail a feed for a gap you already know about and accept.
lesson.l10.rule.null_limit.zero_toleranc: Fail the feed if any row is missing an email
lesson.l10.rule.null_limit.no_check: Skip it - missing emails don't matter
lesson.l10.rule.null_limit.flag_over_5_p: Flag only if the null rate exceeds 5%
lesson.l10.check.referential_integrity.p: Every order should reference a real customer_id. What should this check verify?
lesson.l10.check.referential_integrity.h: A sample can miss a real problem sitting just outside it.
lesson.l10.rule.referential_integrity.sa: Check only the 10 most recent orders
lesson.l10.rule.referential_integrity.no: Skip it - foreign keys are usually fine
lesson.l10.rule.referential_integrity.ch: Check every order against the customer table
lesson.l10.check.freshness.label: Freshness
lesson.l10.check.freshness.prompt: This is meant to be a daily feed. How old should the newest timestamp be allowed to get?
lesson.l10.check.freshness.hint: A rule built for a real-time feed doesn't fit a feed that only updates once a day.
lesson.l10.rule.freshness.flag_over_1_ho: Flag if the latest record is over 1 hour old
lesson.l10.rule.freshness.no_check: Skip it - freshness doesn't matter here
lesson.l10.rule.freshness.flag_over_48_h: Flag if the latest record is over 48 hours old
lesson.l10.check.category_validity.label: Category Validity
lesson.l10.check.category_validity.promp: Status should be one of: pending, shipped, delivered, cancelled. What should this check do?
lesson.l10.check.category_validity.hint: A non-null value can still be an invalid one.
lesson.l10.rule.category_validity.null_o: Only flag rows where status is missing
lesson.l10.rule.category_validity.accept: Accept any value - categories can evolve
lesson.l10.rule.category_validity.flag_u: Flag any value outside the 4 known categories
lesson.l10.field.additional_check_needed: What check would catch what the standard 6 missed here?
Name what would have actually caught it, not just that something was missed.
lesson.l10.option.additional_check_neede: A check that amounts use consistent units
A check that related fields agree with each other
Nothing - the 6 standard checks are enough
lesson.l10.field.validation_principle.hi: Say what validation actually earns you, not just that it's useful.
lesson.l10.option.validation_principle.m: The fix is always more checks, without limit
A human review would have caught it
lesson.l11.title: Distribution Observatory
lesson.l11.objective1: Compare candidate summary statistics against a real histogram
lesson.l11.objective2: Recognize when a single number can't represent the whole population
lesson.l11.objective3: Choose a summary and explain what it hides
lesson.l11.lens.single_number_pick.promp: Leadership wants one number for the typical order value. Which should you show?
lesson.l11.lens.single_number_pick.hint: A few very large orders can pull one of these numbers away from where most orders actually sit.
lesson.l11.lens.spread_pick.prompt: A stakeholder asks how much order values actually vary. What should you report?
lesson.l11.lens.spread_pick.hint: A stable median doesn't mean the underlying values are close together.
lesson.l11.option.spread_pick.highest_or: Point to the single highest order
lesson.l11.option.spread_pick.assume_con: Say it's consistent - the median looks stable
lesson.l11.lens.shape_pick.prompt: Before presenting any single number, what should you actually check?
lesson.l11.lens.shape_pick.hint: A mean or median is computed the same way whether the data forms one cluster or several.
lesson.l11.option.shape_pick.trust_the_m: Nothing - the mean already summarizes it
lesson.l11.option.shape_pick.inspect_the: Check the histogram for multiple clusters
lesson.l11.option.shape_pick.assume_more: Nothing - more data will smooth it out
lesson.l11.field.reporting_approach.prom: Given what the histogram actually shows, how should NovaMart report "typical order value" going forward?
lesson.l11.field.reporting_approach.hint: Say what you'd actually hand to leadership now, not just what's technically correct.
lesson.l11.option.reporting_approach.seg: Report the two segment averages separately
lesson.l11.option.reporting_approach.kee: Keep the overall median - it looked robust
lesson.l11.option.reporting_approach.swi: Switch to the overall mean instead
lesson.l11.field.summary_limitation.prom: What does relying on any single summary number risk hiding?
lesson.l11.field.summary_limitation.hint: Think about what kind of structure no single number can show.
lesson.l11.option.summary_limitation.dis: That the data is really two distinct groups
lesson.l11.option.summary_limitation.not: Nothing, as long as you use the median
Nothing, as long as you collect more data
dialogue.l11_briefing.line1: For the board deck, I just need one number: what's a typical NovaMart order worth?
dialogue.l11_briefing.line2: Keep it simple - mean, median, whatever's standard. One figure.
dialogue.l11_briefing.line3: Before you hand over a number, look at the shape of the data behind it.
dialogue.l11_investigation.line1: Here are order values pulled straight from the order log.
dialogue.l11_investigation.line2: A histogram shows more than any single number can - clusters, gaps, shape.
dialogue.l11_investigation.line3: Let's see what picking different summaries actually does on this chart.
dialogue.l11_independent_intro.line1: Same chart, no hints this time - trust your own read of it.
dialogue.l11_twist.line1: The median looked like a safe, typical figure for the whole feed.
dialogue.l11_twist.line2: Here's what splitting the same data by customer type actually shows.
dialogue.l11_debrief.line1: So the "one number" I wanted was hiding two completely different customers.
dialogue.l11_debrief.line2: A summary isn't wrong for being computed correctly - it's incomplete when the population underneath it isn't one thing.
dialogue.l11_debrief.line3: Robust doesn't mean complete. Always look at the shape before you trust the number.
lesson.l12.title: GroupBy Kitchen
lesson.l12.objective1: Match each request to the right group-by key and aggregation
lesson.l12.objective2: Recognize when grouping at the wrong grain silently double-counts
lesson.l12.objective3: Produce the correct KPI at the grain a stakeholder actually asked for
lesson.l12.pick_both_hint: Pick both to see the result
lesson.l12.request.revenue_per_store.pro: What's total revenue for each store?
lesson.l12.request.revenue_per_store.hin: A store-level total needs one row per store, not per order or per customer.
lesson.l12.request.orders_per_day.prompt: How many orders came in each day?
lesson.l12.request.orders_per_day.hint: Counting orders needs a row per day - grouping too broadly would blur the days together.
lesson.l12.request.average_order_value_p: What's the average order value at each store?
An average combines many orders into one number - counting or summing won't answer "how much, typically".
lesson.l12.twist_title: One Row, One Order - Not One Customer
lesson.l12.field.customer_count_fix.prom: Given what you found, how should NovaMart correctly count customers per store?
lesson.l12.field.customer_count_fix.hint: Say what would actually fix the number, not just that it was wrong.
lesson.l12.option.customer_count_fix.dis: Count distinct customer IDs, per store
lesson.l12.option.customer_count_fix.kee: Keep counting order rows - it's simpler
lesson.l12.field.grouping_risk.prompt: What's the real risk in any groupby result?
lesson.l12.field.grouping_risk.hint: Think about what changes when the grouping key is wrong, not just when the code is wrong.
lesson.l12.option.grouping_risk.wrong_ke: A wrong key silently changes the meaning
lesson.l12.option.grouping_risk.groupby_: None - a groupby result is correct by definition
lesson.l12.option.grouping_risk.only_mat: It only matters once the dataset is very large
dialogue.l12_briefing.line1: Ops wants a few numbers before Friday: revenue per store, orders per day, average order value per store.
dialogue.l12_briefing.line2: Just wire up the right group-by for each and pull the numbers.
dialogue.l12_briefing.line3: Same data, three different questions - each one needs its own grain.
dialogue.l12_investigation.line1: Here's the raw order log - one row per order, with a store, a customer, and a date.
dialogue.l12_investigation.line2: Group by the wrong column and you still get a real number - just not the one anyone asked for.
dialogue.l12_investigation.line3: Watch how the result table itself changes shape as you pick a different grain.
dialogue.l12_independent_intro.line1: Same three requests, no hints this time.
dialogue.l12_twist.line1: Someone already ran "customers per store" for the quarterly report.
dialogue.l12_twist.line2: Here's what happened when that number was checked against actual distinct customers.
dialogue.l12_debrief.line1: Store S02 wasn't a ten-customer success story - it was four people ordering a lot.
dialogue.l12_debrief.line2: Grouping by the wrong key doesn't fail loudly. It just quietly answers a different question.
dialogue.l12_debrief.line3: Always ask what one row in your result actually represents.
lesson.l13.title: Join Junction
lesson.l13.objective1: Pick the join type that actually answers each request
lesson.l13.objective2: See how inner, left, and right joins disagree on row count
lesson.l13.objective3: Repair a join and prove its totals are still valid
lesson.l13.pick_a_join_hint: Pick a join type to see the result
lesson.l13.request.orders_missing_custom: We need every order, even the ones we can't match to a customer record yet.
Keeping every order means the left table can't lose rows, whatever happens on the right.
lesson.l13.request.confident_customer_ma: We only want orders where we're confident about who the customer is.
Only rows with a real match on both sides survive this one.
lesson.l13.request.full_customer_outreac: Marketing wants the full customer list, including everyone who's never ordered.
Keeping every customer means the right table can't lose rows, whatever happens on the left.
lesson.l13.field.revenue_repair.prompt: How should NovaMart safely total revenue despite customers having multiple active promotions?
lesson.l13.field.revenue_repair.hint: Say what actually keeps each order counted once, not just that the old number was wrong.
lesson.l13.option.revenue_repair.sum_fro: Sum revenue from the original orders table
lesson.l13.option.revenue_repair.divide_: Sum after the join, then divide by promo count
lesson.l13.option.revenue_repair.pick_on: Keep one promotion per customer, then join
lesson.l13.field.join_lesson.prompt: What's the general lesson about joins and totals?
lesson.l13.field.join_lesson.hint: Think about what a join can do to row count, not just which columns it adds.
lesson.l13.option.join_lesson.verify_aft: Verify row counts and totals after every join
lesson.l13.option.join_lesson.joins_neve: Joins only add columns, never change totals
lesson.l13.option.join_lesson.only_many_: Only many-to-many joins are ever risky
dialogue.l13_briefing.line1: We need orders, customers, and promotions combined for the campaign report.
dialogue.l13_briefing.line2: Just join the tables - shouldn't take long.
dialogue.l13_briefing.line3: Which rows survive a join depends entirely on which join you pick.
dialogue.l13_investigation.line1: Here's customers and orders - they only partially overlap on customer_id.
dialogue.l13_investigation.line2: Some orders have no matching customer. Some customers have never ordered.
dialogue.l13_investigation.line3: Watch which nodes drop out as you switch join types.
dialogue.l13_independent_intro.line1: Same three requests, no hints this time.
dialogue.l13_twist.line1: Someone already joined orders to active promotions and summed the revenue column.
dialogue.l13_twist.line2: Here's what that number looks like next to the orders table's own total.
dialogue.l13_debrief.line1: Two customers had more than one active promotion - their orders got counted twice, three times.
dialogue.l13_debrief.line2: A join can multiply rows without ever touching a wrong value.
dialogue.l13_debrief.line3: Check row counts and totals after every join - not just once, every time.
lesson.l14.title: Chart Designer
lesson.l14.objective1: Match each question to a chart type that actually fits it
lesson.l14.objective2: See how axis scale can exaggerate or hide a real difference
lesson.l14.objective3: Choose the chart that answers the question without misleading
lesson.l14.pick_a_chart_hint: Pick a chart to see the preview
lesson.l14.option.bar_zoomed: Bar chart, axis zoomed to the data
lesson.l14.request.revenue_by_store.prom: Compare total revenue across our three stores this month.
lesson.l14.request.revenue_by_store.hint: The stores aren't an ordered sequence - a line between them would imply a trend that isn't there.
lesson.l14.request.daily_revenue_trend.p: Show how revenue moved day by day this week.

lesson.l14.request.returns_by_store.prom: Compare how many returns each store logged this month.
lesson.l14.request.returns_by_store.hint: Zooming the axis would make a real gap between stores look far bigger than it is.
lesson.l14.field.correct_return_metric.p: Given what the rates show, how should NovaMart report store return performance?
