A zoomed axis always makes trends clearer
dialogue.l14_briefing.line1: We need charts for the store review meeting - revenue by store, the weekly trend, and returns.
dialogue.l14_briefing.line2: Whatever looks clearest is fine - just make the numbers pop.
dialogue.l14_briefing.line3: The chart type and the scale aren't decoration - they change what the audience actually concludes.
dialogue.l14_investigation.line1: Same underlying numbers can look completely different depending on how you draw them.
dialogue.l14_investigation.line2: A chart type built for one kind of question can lie about another.
dialogue.l14_investigation.line3: Watch what happens to the same three bars when the axis changes.
dialogue.l14_independent_intro.line1: Same three requests, no hints this time.
dialogue.l14_twist.line1: The returns chart made S02 look like the problem store - it had the most raw returns.
dialogue.l14_twist.line2: Here's the same three stores by return rate instead.
dialogue.l14_debrief.line1: So the store with the most returns actually has the best rate. That would've gone into the report wrong.
dialogue.l14_debrief.line2: A chart can be completely accurate and still tell the wrong story, if it's answering the wrong question.
dialogue.l14_debrief.line3: Before trusting a chart, ask what's being counted - and what it's being counted out of.
lesson.l15.title: Segment Detective
lesson.l15.objective1: Slice a metric by the dimension that actually checks a specific complaint
lesson.l15.objective2: Recognize Simpson's paradox: every segment can decline while the total improves
lesson.l15.objective3: Explain the discrepancy and identify the right level of analysis
lesson.l15.pick_a_slice_hint: Pick a dimension to see the breakdown
lesson.l15.request.mobile_conversion_com: The mobile team says their conversion rate got worse this quarter.
Check the dimension that actually contains a "mobile" segment.
lesson.l15.request.eu_region_complaint.p: The EU region team says their conversion rate got worse this quarter.
lesson.l15.request.eu_region_complaint.h: Check the dimension that actually contains an "EU" segment.
lesson.l15.request.paid_channel_complain: The paid-ads team says their conversion rate got worse this quarter.
Check the dimension that actually contains a "paid ads" segment.
lesson.l15.field.correct_level_of_analys: Given what you found, what's the right level to report NovaMart's performance at?
Say what a leader would actually need to see both numbers for.
lesson.l15.option.correct_level_of_analy: Report both the total and the segments
Trust the segments - the aggregate misleads
lesson.l15.field.paradox_lesson.hint: Think about what changed between the two quarters besides the rates themselves.
lesson.l15.option.paradox_lesson.mix_shi: A mix shift can hide real segment declines
lesson.l15.option.paradox_lesson.aggrega: The total is wrong if segments disagree
lesson.l15.option.paradox_lesson.only_ma: This only happens with two segments
dialogue.l15_briefing.line1: Leadership's happy - our overall conversion rate is up this quarter.
dialogue.l15_briefing.line2: But three different teams are telling me their own numbers got worse. That can't both be true.
dialogue.l15_briefing.line3: It can. It usually means something about the mix changed, not just the rates.
dialogue.l15_investigation.line1: Here's conversion data broken out by device, region, and acquisition channel.
dialogue.l15_investigation.line2: Each team is only asking about their own slice - pull the right one and check their number directly.
dialogue.l15_investigation.line3: Notice what happens to each segment's own rate before you look at anything else.
dialogue.l15_independent_intro.line1: Same three complaints, no hints this time.
dialogue.l15_twist.line1: Every team you checked was right - their own segment's rate really did go down.
dialogue.l15_twist.line2: Here's the same period's company-wide rate, the number leadership actually saw.
dialogue.l15_debrief.line1: So we were both right. My number went up. Their numbers went down. At the same time.
dialogue.l15_debrief.line2: The traffic mix shifted toward a segment that converts better - even as it also declined.
dialogue.l15_debrief.line3: A total can move for reasons that have nothing to do with anything actually improving.
lesson.l16.title: Metric Forge
lesson.l16.objective1: Pick a target metric that resists gaming, not just one that moves fast
lesson.l16.objective2: Watch a narrow target improve while its own guardrail quietly breaks
lesson.l16.objective3: Design a metric system built on one primary metric plus real guardrails
lesson.l16.pick_a_metric_hint: Pick a metric to see how the team responds
lesson.l16.request.support_speed_initiat: Support wants to close tickets faster. Which metric should be the official target?
A metric that rewards speed alone can be hit without solving anything.
lesson.l16.request.sales_growth_initiati: Sales wants to grow monthly signups. Which metric should be the official target?
More signups isn't the same as more customers who stick around.
lesson.l16.request.app_engagement_initia: The app team wants to boost daily engagement. Which metric should be the official target?
Opening the app isn't the same as the app being useful.
lesson.l16.twist_churn_before_label: Customer churn rate before the initiative
lesson.l16.twist_churn_after_label: Customer churn rate one quarter later
lesson.l16.field.metric_system_design.pr: Given what happened, how should NovaMart set up its metric system for the next initiative?
lesson.l16.field.metric_system_design.hi: Say what would have actually caught the problem in time.
lesson.l16.option.metric_system_design.p: One primary metric and tracked guardrails
Only the best primary metric - skip guardrails
lesson.l16.option.metric_system_design.m: Many metrics tracked equally, no primary
lesson.l16.field.goodhart_lesson.hint: Think about what happens to any number once people are rewarded for moving it.
lesson.l16.option.goodhart_lesson.any_ta: Any metric can be gamed once made a target
lesson.l16.option.goodhart_lesson.only_b: Only obviously bad metrics get gamed
dialogue.l16_briefing.line1: We're launching a support initiative and need one official success metric.
dialogue.l16_briefing.line2: Keep it simple - the board wants one number to watch, not a dashboard.
dialogue.l16_briefing.line3: Whatever you choose, the team will optimize exactly that - not the intent behind it.
dialogue.l16_investigation.line1: Here's what happened the last few times a metric like this became an official target.
dialogue.l16_investigation.line2: The target number always moves. What matters is what happens beside it.
dialogue.l16_investigation.line3: Pick a metric and watch its own guardrail react.
dialogue.l16_independent_intro.line1: Same three initiatives, no hints this time.
dialogue.l16_twist.line1: Support already picked a speed metric last quarter, before any of this was checked.
dialogue.l16_twist.line2: Nobody was watching customer churn - here's what it did in the meantime.
dialogue.l16_debrief.line1: So the number we were watching looked great this whole time.
dialogue.l16_debrief.line2: A guardrail only helps if someone actually assigns one before the target ships.
dialogue.l16_debrief.line3: The metric isn't the goal. It's a proxy for the goal - and proxies break under pressure.
lesson.l17.title: Hypothesis Detective
lesson.l17.objective1: Predict a metric's direction before seeing any data, not after
lesson.l17.objective2: Recognize an attractive after-the-fact explanation for what it is
lesson.l17.objective3: Separate what you pre-specified from what you noticed afterward
Will one-click reorder change the repeat purchase rate?
Removing friction from reordering usually pulls this one way.
lesson.l17.request.average_order_value.p: Will one-click reorder change the average order value?
lesson.l17.request.average_order_value.h: Think about what a one-click repeat order actually tends to contain.
Will one-click reorder change the support contact rate?
A reorder button doesn't touch anything support usually deals with.
lesson.l17.twist_app_before_label: App users' repeat purchase rate before launch
lesson.l17.twist_app_after_label: App users' repeat purchase rate after launch
lesson.l17.twist_website_before_label: Website users' repeat purchase rate before launch
lesson.l17.twist_website_after_label: Website users' repeat purchase rate after launch
lesson.l17.field.posthoc_pattern_respons: Given what you found, what should the team do with the app-vs-website pattern?
Say what a pattern needs before anyone should act on it.
lesson.l17.option.posthoc_pattern_respon: Announce it as the confirmed reason for the win
Treat it as a new hypothesis, test it properly
Ignore it - only pre-specified results ever count
lesson.l17.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what happens once you've already seen the outcome.
lesson.l17.option.general_lesson.only_co: Only the most confident prediction matters
lesson.l17.option.general_lesson.big_eno: A big enough pattern doesn't need testing
lesson.l17.option.general_lesson.posthoc: An after-the-fact pattern needs its own test
dialogue.l17_briefing.line1: We just shipped one-click reorder, and I think it's changing how customers behave.
dialogue.l17_briefing.line2: Before we celebrate anything, I want real predictions on the table - not a victory lap after the fact.
dialogue.l17_briefing.line3: Good instinct. Write down what you expect before you look at a single number.
dialogue.l17_investigation.line1: Here are three things one-click reorder could plausibly move.
dialogue.l17_investigation.line2: Predict a direction for each one before revealing it - no peeking at the data first.
dialogue.l17_investigation.line3: Once a prediction is revealed, it's locked in - no editing it after seeing the truth.
dialogue.l17_independent_intro.line1: Same three predictions, no hints this time.
dialogue.l17_twist.line1: Repeat purchases are up - and someone's already spotted why: "it's obviously the app users."
dialogue.l17_twist.line2: Here's that same rate split by device, before and after launch.
dialogue.l17_debrief.line1: So app users are miles ahead of website users. That's the story, right?
dialogue.l17_debrief.line2: They were already miles ahead before launch. Both groups moved by the exact same amount.
dialogue.l17_debrief.line3: That split was never a hypothesis - it's a story built after seeing the result, and the numbers don't actually back it.
lesson.l18.title: Randomization Control Room
lesson.l18.objective1: Check group size, not just assume a rule is random because it looks arbitrary
lesson.l18.objective2: Recognize that a clean sample-ratio check doesn't rule out a biased split
lesson.l18.objective3: Decide whether a flawed experiment should be approved, repaired, or invalidated
lesson.l18.pick_a_rule_hint: Pick a rule to see its real balance diagnostics
lesson.l18.request.checkout_redesign.pro: Checkout redesign: which assignment rule should this experiment use?
lesson.l18.request.checkout_redesign.hin: This redesign only touches the mobile checkout flow.
lesson.l18.request.loyalty_discount_test: Loyalty discount test: which assignment rule should this experiment use?
Referral customers tend to behave differently around discounts.
lesson.l18.request.notification_frequenc: Notification frequency test: which assignment rule should this experiment use?
High-spend customers tend to react differently to being messaged more.
lesson.l18.field.experiment_verdict.prom: Given what the platform split shows, what should happen to the referral bonus rollout's results?
lesson.l18.field.experiment_verdict.hint: Say what group size alone did and didn't actually prove.
lesson.l18.option.experiment_verdict.app: Approve the results - group size was enough
lesson.l18.option.experiment_verdict.rep: Repair the rule, then rerun the experiment
lesson.l18.option.experiment_verdict.inv: Invalidate it completely and drop the idea
lesson.l18.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what a sample-ratio check can and can't catch.
lesson.l18.option.general_lesson.any_spl: Any split is fine if the group sizes match
lesson.l18.option.general_lesson.srm_pas: Matching group sizes doesn't rule out bias
dialogue.l18_briefing.line1: We're about to run three product experiments, and I need the assignment set up correctly before any of them launch.
dialogue.l18_briefing.line2: Whoever wrote these candidate rules swears each one is basically random. Let's actually check that.
dialogue.l18_briefing.line3: A clean group-size check is the bare minimum, not the whole story.
dialogue.l18_investigation.line1: Here's what each rule actually assigns, for real, on this experiment's own customers.
dialogue.l18_investigation.line2: Group size can look perfect and still hide a real problem in who ended up where.
dialogue.l18_investigation.line3: Pick a rule and check group size plus the one attribute this experiment actually depends on.
dialogue.l18_independent_intro.line1: Same three experiments, no hints this time.
dialogue.l18_twist.line1: NovaMart already shipped a referral bonus rollout using customer ID parity - group size passed clean, so the team called it done.
dialogue.l18_twist.line2: Nobody checked platform. Here's what a migration-era ID bug did to it.
dialogue.l18_debrief.line1: So the numbers from that rollout might not mean what we thought they meant.
dialogue.l18_debrief.line2: A platform migration years ago handed out IDs in blocks - iOS customers mostly landed on one side of the split by accident.
dialogue.l18_debrief.line3: A sample-ratio check catches missing people. It doesn't catch the wrong people ending up on the wrong side.
lesson.l19.title: Power Plant
lesson.l19.objective1: Allocate limited weeks across experiments, not just split time evenly
lesson.l19.objective2: Read a detectable-effect number as a direct consequence of sample size
lesson.l19.objective3: Recognize that a real, detected effect can still be too small to matter
lesson.l19.allocator_prompt: Spend the quarter's weeks across these three experiments.
lesson.l19.allocator_hint: Watch the detectable-effect number under each row - that's what your allocation actually buys.
lesson.l19.twist_title: What a Full Quarter Actually Bought
Given the banner experiment's real 1-point lift, what should NovaMart do?
Say what a real effect still needs before it's worth shipping.
lesson.l19.option.banner_result_response: Ship it - a real, detected effect is worth acting on
Don't ship it - real, but below the bar
Run it longer - a bigger sample grows the effect
lesson.l19.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what a bigger sample can and can't change about an effect.
lesson.l19.option.general_lesson.bigger_: A bigger sample is always worth the extra time
lesson.l19.option.general_lesson.undetec: If an effect isn't detected, it doesn't exist
lesson.l19.option.general_lesson.statist: Statistically real isn't the same as important
dialogue.l19_briefing.line1: We've got a quarter of runway and three experiments competing for it. I need a plan, not three wishlists.
dialogue.l19_briefing.line2: Every extra week we spend testing is a week we're not shipping something else.
dialogue.l19_briefing.line3: More weeks means more traffic means a smaller effect you could actually detect. That's the real trade-off - not just 'more is better.'
dialogue.l19_investigation.line1: Each experiment has its own traffic level and its own bar for what's actually worth shipping.
dialogue.l19_investigation.line2: A high-traffic page needs fewer weeks per point of sensitivity - but a strict bar can still make it the most expensive to satisfy.
dialogue.l19_investigation.line3: Watch the detectable-effect number under each row as you spend weeks - that's what your allocation actually buys.
dialogue.l19_independent_intro.line1: Same quarter, same three experiments, no hints this time.
dialogue.l19_twist.line1: NovaMart already ran a homepage banner experiment - a full quarter, full site traffic, the biggest sample this team has ever collected.
dialogue.l19_twist.line2: Here's exactly what that bought them.
dialogue.l19_debrief.line1: A real 1-point lift, and we can actually trust it's real. So we ship it, right?
dialogue.l19_debrief.line2: Real and worth shipping aren't the same question. Homepage changes need at least a 2-point lift to clear the engineering cost.
dialogue.l19_debrief.line3: With enough traffic, almost anything becomes detectable. The only question that matters is whether it's big enough to be worth it.
lesson.l20.title: A/B Test Commander
lesson.l20.objective1: Watch a live experiment dashboard across checkpoints, not just once
lesson.l20.objective2: Recognize that an early lead can be real-looking and still not hold
lesson.l20.objective3: Choose ship, don't ship, or run longer - and justify it
lesson.l20.dashboard_hint: An early lead is real data - it's just not the whole story yet.
lesson.l20.twist_title: The Peek That Pointed the Wrong Way
lesson.l20.field.checkout_experiment_ver: Given the full 21-day checkout experiment result, what should NovaMart do?
Say what the full, planned sample actually showed.
lesson.l20.option.checkout_experiment_ve: Don't ship it - a lift this small isn't worth it
Ship it - the full run shows a small, stable, real lift
Run it even longer - we haven't seen enough yet
lesson.l20.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about which direction an early, noisy read can point.
lesson.l20.option.general_lesson.more_da: More data just confirms the early read
lesson.l20.option.general_lesson.stoppin: Stopping early only risks missing a real win
lesson.l20.option.general_lesson.peeking: A peek can look like a win and still be wrong
dialogue.l20_briefing.line1: The checkout experiment just crossed day 3, and the early numbers look great. Are we ready to call it?
dialogue.l20_briefing.line2: We planned this to run 21 days. Three days in is still a tiny sample.
dialogue.l20_briefing.line3: Watch the dashboard the whole way through - notice how much the story can still change before day 21.
dialogue.l20_investigation.line1: At every checkpoint, you can stop and decide now, or keep running to the next one.
dialogue.l20_investigation.line2: An early lead is real data - it's just not yet the whole story.
dialogue.l20_investigation.line3: Watch the guardrails too - a clean primary metric doesn't mean nothing else moved.
dialogue.l20_independent_intro.line1: Same experiment, same checkpoints, no hints this time.
dialogue.l20_twist.line1: NovaMart already shipped a different change - a search re-ranking test - on the strength of a promising day-4 peek.
dialogue.l20_twist.line2: Here's what that same change actually did once it had been live at full scale for a while.
dialogue.l20_debrief.line1: So the numbers that got us excited on day 4 weren't just optimistic. They pointed the wrong way completely.
dialogue.l20_debrief.line2: An early sample can be noisy in either direction. There's no way to know which, from inside the noise.
dialogue.l20_debrief.line3: The fix isn't fancier math - it's just waiting for the sample you already planned for.
lesson.l21.title: Funnel Factory
lesson.l21.objective1: Build a funnel from raw events, not just accept one that's handed to you
lesson.l21.objective2: Recognize that changing a funnel's definition can change its apparent bottleneck
lesson.l21.objective3: Identify the most defensible drop-off and propose what to check next
lesson.l21.request.mobile_dropout_compla: Marketing says most people bounce right after viewing a product, before ever adding anything to cart.
Check whether the cart step is actually being counted completely.
lesson.l21.request.payment_step_complain: Ops says the payment step is where NovaMart loses everyone.
A step's share of total visits and its own local conversion rate are different questions.
lesson.l21.request.cart_abandonment_comp: Someone claims people abandon their cart before ever starting checkout.
Check whether the cart count is counting sessions or every click.
lesson.l21.twist_title: The Quarter Spent Fixing the Wrong Thing
lesson.l21.twist_flawed_signup_label: Onboarding - signup rate (the count the team used)
lesson.l21.field.checkout_investigation_: Given every defensible funnel definition, what's the real story behind NovaMart's checkout drop-off?
Say which step holds up as the worst one across the defensible definitions, not just one convenient reading.
lesson.l21.option.checkout_investigation: People bounce right after viewing a product
The real drop is between cart and checkout
The payment step itself is failing
lesson.l21.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what should justify a funnel definition in the first place.
lesson.l21.option.general_lesson.any_def: Any funnel definition is equally valid
lesson.l21.option.general_lesson.more_de: More tested definitions means more accuracy
lesson.l21.option.general_lesson.justify: A definition needs its own logic, not its result
dialogue.l21_briefing.line1: Checkout conversion is down and everyone has a theory about why. I need an actual funnel, not another guess.
dialogue.l21_briefing.line2: We have the raw events. How we turn them into a funnel is a real design decision, not just a formality.
dialogue.l21_briefing.line3: The same events can tell three different stories, depending on how each step gets defined.
dialogue.l21_investigation.line1: Each complaint below points at a different step. Check whether a defensible funnel actually backs it up.
dialogue.l21_investigation.line2: Watch for a step that converts suspiciously well right after one that converts suspiciously badly - that's often a sign the count itself is broken.
dialogue.l21_investigation.line3: Pick the definition you'd actually be willing to defend, not just the one that confirms the complaint.
dialogue.l21_independent_intro.line1: Same three complaints, no hints this time.
dialogue.l21_twist.line1: The app team already investigated a different funnel - onboarding - using a signup-completion event with a known gap.
dialogue.l21_twist.line2: Here's what a properly counted funnel actually showed, after they'd already spent a quarter fixing the wrong thing.
dialogue.l21_debrief.line1: So they redesigned signup, and signup was never the real problem.
dialogue.l21_debrief.line2: A gap in one tracking pixel made a healthy step look broken, and hid a genuinely broken one right behind it.
dialogue.l21_debrief.line3: The fix isn't a better-looking chart - it's being able to say exactly why this definition, and not another, is the one to trust.
lesson.l22.title: Cohort Observatory
lesson.l22.objective1: Read a cohort matrix as a whole, not just its most exciting cell
lesson.l22.objective2: Recognize that a newer cohort simply hasn't had time to churn yet
lesson.l22.objective3: State whether retention actually improved, and for which cohorts
lesson.l22.option.mismatched_month_compa: Compare best month vs. worst month
lesson.l22.option.same_month_comparison: Compare the same month for both
lesson.l22.request.newest_cohort_claim.p: Leadership says the May cohort's Month 1 retention beats every older cohort - retention is clearly improving.
lesson.l22.request.newest_cohort_claim.h: Only compare cohorts at the same number of months since they joined.
lesson.l22.request.april_complaint.promp: Someone claims the April cohort is underperforming - worse retention than everyone else.
lesson.l22.request.april_complaint.hint: Check April against every other cohort's own number at the same age, not a later, more-decayed one.
lesson.l22.request.march_product_change_: Someone says a product change in March improved retention for everyone who joined that month.
March can only be fairly compared to February at the ages both cohorts actually share.
lesson.l22.twist_title: The Cohort That Looked Like a Winner
lesson.l22.twist_november_month1_label: November cohort - Month 1 (when it was the newest cohort)
lesson.l22.twist_january_month1_label: January cohort - Month 1 (what it was being compared to)
lesson.l22.twist_november_month5_label: November cohort - Month 5 (now that it's fully observed)
lesson.l22.field.retention_verdict.promp: Given everything you've seen, has retention really improved?
lesson.l22.field.retention_verdict.hint: Say what you can and can't actually know yet from an immature cohort.
lesson.l22.option.retention_verdict.yes_: Yes - the newest cohorts retain better
lesson.l22.option.retention_verdict.too_: Too early - only mature cohorts compare fairly
lesson.l22.option.retention_verdict.no_c: No - retention has clearly gotten worse
lesson.l22.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what a cohort's early number can and can't tell you yet.
lesson.l22.option.general_lesson.newer_a: The newest cohort's early numbers matter most
lesson.l22.option.general_lesson.once_a_: A good early cohort usually stays good
lesson.l22.option.general_lesson.same_ag: Cohorts are only comparable at the same age
dialogue.l22_briefing.line1: NovaMart Plus leadership is thrilled - the newest customers are retaining better than ever. I want that in the board deck.
dialogue.l22_briefing.line2: Just confirm the numbers before I put a headline on them.
dialogue.l22_briefing.line3: A cohort's numbers aren't finished until enough time has actually passed to see them.
dialogue.l22_investigation.line1: This is a real cohort retention matrix - each row only has data for however many months have actually passed since it joined.
dialogue.l22_investigation.line2: A newer cohort's early numbers can only be fairly compared to an older cohort's numbers at that same age - not its later, more-decayed ones.
dialogue.l22_investigation.line3: Pick the comparison you'd actually stand behind for each claim.
dialogue.l22_independent_intro.line1: Same three claims, no hints this time.
dialogue.l22_twist.line1: The November cohort once looked exactly like this - a standout Month 1 number, ahead of everything before it.
dialogue.l22_twist.line2: Here's what it actually settled at, now that there's finally been enough time to know.
dialogue.l22_debrief.line1: So November looked like our best cohort ever, and it ended up below average.
dialogue.l22_debrief.line2: At Month 1, nobody could have told the difference between a real improvement and a cohort that just hadn't decayed yet.
dialogue.l22_debrief.line3: The only honest answer this early is 'not yet known' - not yes, and not no.
lesson.l23.title: Time Series Control Room
lesson.l23.objective1: Read a daily time series without over-reacting to the days right next to an event
lesson.l23.objective2: Compare a suspicious change to the same calendar days from before it
lesson.l23.objective3: Tell a real effect apart from ordinary calendar noise like weekends and releases
lesson.l23.option.nearby_days_only: Look at the days right around it
lesson.l23.option.same_days_previous_per: Compare to the same days, previous period
lesson.l23.request.release_dip_claim.pro: The release shipped right before checkout conversion dropped on Saturday and Sunday. Leadership wants to know if the release caused it.
lesson.l23.request.release_dip_claim.hin: Weekends always run lower than weekdays - check whether this weekend actually looks different from a normal one.
lesson.l23.request.campaign_lift_claim.p: Marketing says Monday's campaign really moved conversion. Check whether that lift is real.
lesson.l23.request.campaign_lift_claim.h: A campaign Monday and an ordinary Monday are the fair comparison - not the weekend right before it.
Someone flags that conversion 'declined' this week compared to last week. Check whether that's a real trend.
Last week had a campaign in it. Compare this week to a normal week, not to an inflated one.
lesson.l23.twist_title: The 2am Page That Wasn't a Bug
lesson.l23.twist_alert_day_label: Day after the holiday (when the page went out)
lesson.l23.twist_repeat_holiday_label: Day after a different holiday, same pattern
lesson.l23.twist_recovered_label: Two days later, no fix applied
lesson.l23.field.escalation_verdict.prom: Given everything you found, what actually deserves escalation?
lesson.l23.field.escalation_verdict.hint: Not every change near an event was caused by that event - and not every real change is bad news.
lesson.l23.option.escalation_verdict.no_: No - it was all calendar noise
lesson.l23.option.escalation_verdict.yes: Yes - but only the campaign result
Yes - all three are real changes
lesson.l23.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what actually makes two days a fair comparison.
lesson.l23.option.general_lesson.any_dip: A nearby dip means the event caused it
lesson.l23.option.general_lesson.always_: Always compare to the same calendar days
dialogue.l23_briefing.line1: Checkout conversion just dropped and I need an explanation before the exec meeting.
dialogue.l23_briefing.line2: We shipped a release right around then. Might be that.

lesson.l24.title: Survey Bureau
lesson.l24.objective1: Design a survey question that doesn't push the answer in either direction
lesson.l24.objective2: Recognize when a recruitment channel can't reach an entire group of customers
lesson.l24.objective3: Interpret a survey's results without claiming they represent every customer
lesson.l24.twist_title: The Survey That Couldn't Hear Everyone
lesson.l24.request.general_satisfaction_: Leadership wants an honest overall read on reaction to the price change, for the board deck.
Pick a wording that doesn't push answers in either direction, and a channel that doesn't only reach your happiest customers.
lesson.l24.request.fast_turnaround_tempt: The board meets tomorrow. Marketing already has an upbeat version of the question ready, and the in-app popup could go out today.
Fast and ready isn't the same as sound - the in-app popup can't reach anyone who already quit over the change.
lesson.l24.request.advisory_panel_tempta: Someone suggests just asking the loyalty advisory panel - they're engaged and always give thoughtful feedback.
The panel is thoughtful precisely because it's your most satisfied, most engaged customers - not because it's representative.
lesson.l24.twist_never_surveyed_label: Customers never surveyed at all (delivery failed or delayed)
lesson.l24.twist_blended_label: True rate across every customer, once both groups count
lesson.l24.field.survey_interpretation.p: How should the survey results actually be presented to leadership?
lesson.l24.field.survey_interpretation.h: Think about who could never have ended up in that sample, no matter how it was worded.
Exactly how satisfied all customers are
A useful signal, not proof of everyone
Nothing useful - throw the survey out
lesson.l24.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what a bigger sample can and can't fix.
lesson.l24.option.general_lesson.bigger_: A bigger sample always fixes response bias
lesson.l24.option.general_lesson.who_res: Who responds is never a random slice
lesson.l24.option.general_lesson.wording: Wording only matters if obviously biased
dialogue.l24_briefing.line1: Reaction to the price change is all over the place. I need a real number before the board meeting.
dialogue.l24_briefing.line2: Marketing already has a channel and a question ready to go.
dialogue.l24_briefing.line3: Ready isn't the same as sound. How you ask and who you ask both change the answer you get.
dialogue.l24_investigation.line1: Every design here draws from the same real customer population - only the wording and the channel change.
dialogue.l24_investigation.line2: Watch the respondent count, not just the average - a channel that quietly excludes people is still bias, even with plenty of responses left.
dialogue.l24_investigation.line3: Pick the wording and channel you'd actually stand behind for each scenario.

dialogue.l24_debrief.line1: So a bigger response count wouldn't have fixed the delivery survey at all.
dialogue.l24_debrief.line2: No - the problem was who could never be asked in the first place, not how many answered.
dialogue.l24_debrief.line3: Report what you found, but say plainly who it can't speak for.
lesson.l25.title: KPI Emergency Room
lesson.l25.objective1: Choose a north-star metric that actually reflects a real problem
lesson.l25.objective2: Set an alert threshold that catches real incidents without drowning in noise
lesson.l25.objective3: Design a compact monitoring system instead of watching everything at once
lesson.l25.request.checkout_incident_foc: Checkout conversion had an unexplained spike in errors this month. Set up a monitor that would have actually caught it.
The metric that actually moves during the incident matters more than how tightly you watch it.
lesson.l25.request.delivery_incident_foc: On-time delivery quietly cratered for a day, and nobody noticed until customers complained. Design a monitor that wouldn't have missed it.
A metric that never reflects the problem won't catch it, no matter how tight the threshold.
lesson.l25.request.monitor_everything_te: Someone wants every metric watched with the tightest possible threshold, 'just to be safe.'
Tight thresholds on noisy metrics mostly produce alert fatigue, not safety.
lesson.l25.twist_real_incident_count_lab: Genuinely real incidents that same month
lesson.l25.twist_false_alarm_response_la: Typical time to dismiss a false alarm (minutes)
lesson.l25.twist_real_incident_response_: Time to notice the one real incident (minutes)
lesson.l25.field.system_verdict.prompt: What does a genuinely good monitoring system look like here?
lesson.l25.field.system_verdict.hint: Think about what actually caught this quarter's two real incidents.
lesson.l25.option.system_verdict.every_m: Every metric, watched as tight as possible
lesson.l25.option.system_verdict.a_few_m: A few well-chosen metrics, sensible thresholds
lesson.l25.option.system_verdict.one_eas: One easy metric, even if just for show
lesson.l25.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what more alerts actually bought you this quarter.
lesson.l25.option.general_lesson.tighter: A tighter threshold always catches more
lesson.l25.option.general_lesson.more_al: More alerts is not the same as better monitoring
lesson.l25.option.general_lesson.which_m: Which metric matters less than coverage
dialogue.l25_briefing.line1: You've inherited the ops dashboard. Forty-plus metrics, alerts firing constantly, nobody trusts any of them anymore.
dialogue.l25_briefing.line2: Two real incidents actually happened this quarter. A working monitor should have caught both without the noise.
dialogue.l25_briefing.line3: Then let's design one properly - which metric you watch matters as much as how tightly you watch it.
dialogue.l25_investigation.line1: This is the real 14-day log behind each incident - a metric that never moves during a real problem won't catch it no matter how you tune it.
dialogue.l25_investigation.line2: A tight threshold on a genuinely noisy metric mostly just produces false alarms, not safety.
dialogue.l25_investigation.line3: Pick the metric and threshold you'd actually stand behind for each scenario.
dialogue.l25_independent_intro.line1: Same three scenarios, no hints this time.
dialogue.l25_twist.line1: Warehouse Ops fired 47 alerts last month - 46 of them meant nothing.
dialogue.l25_twist.line2: Here's what happened the one time it actually mattered.
dialogue.l25_debrief.line1: So watching more metrics, tighter, wouldn't have helped at all.
dialogue.l25_debrief.line2: It would have made things worse - more noise, not more safety.
dialogue.l25_debrief.line3: A compact system built on metrics that actually move is worth more than a dashboard that never stops ringing.
lesson.l26.title: Correlation Crime Scene
lesson.l26.objective1: Recognize that a real correlation doesn't establish which explanation is true
lesson.l26.objective2: Identify which alternative explanations survive, and which are actually ruled out
lesson.l26.objective3: State what's supported by the evidence and what would actually settle the question
lesson.l26.twist_title: The Gap That Wasn't the Program
lesson.l26.request.push_opens_claim.prom: Push opens and weekly spend move together like this. Marketing says notifications are clearly driving the spend.
lesson.l26.request.push_opens_claim.hint: Ask what would actually distinguish 'A causes B' from 'B causes A' from 'something else causes both' - then check whether that evidence exists here.
lesson.l26.evidence.push_opens_claim: This same pattern holds for every one of the customers tracked - no exceptions.
lesson.l26.option.push_opens_claim.coinc: Coincidence is ruled out - which one's the real cause isn't
lesson.l26.option.push_opens_claim.prove: This proves notifications are increasing spend
lesson.l26.option.push_opens_claim.nothi: With correlation alone, nothing at all can be concluded
Right - a pattern this consistent is unlikely to be chance. But correlation alone can't say whether opens drive spend, spend drives opens, or something else drives both.
Correlation alone can't prove which direction the arrow points, or whether a third factor explains both.
A pattern this consistent across every customer tracked is unlikely to be pure chance - that much is actually supported.
Shipment days and daily sales move together like this. Ops says the delivery schedule is obviously driving the spikes.
Check whether the timing itself is even capable of running in reverse.
lesson.l26.evidence.shipment_sales_claim: The shipment calendar is fixed by logistics months in advance, completely independent of real-time sales.
lesson.l26.option.shipment_sales_claim.r: Reverse causation is still just as plausible as the others
Reverse causation is ruled out - direct causation and a hidden factor both remain open
lesson.l26.option.shipment_sales_claim.m: Sales can't cause the shipment, so the shipment must be causing the sales
lesson.l26.explanation.shipment_sales_cl: The shipment schedule is fixed months ahead, independent of sales - it genuinely cannot be a reaction to them.
Right - the calendar can't be reacting to sales that haven't happened yet. But the shipment itself boosting sales, or something else driving both, are both still live.
Ruling out one direction doesn't prove the other - a hidden factor could still explain both without either causing the other.
lesson.l26.request.dark_mode_claim.promp: Dark mode users spend more like this. Someone on the design team says dark mode is clearly driving the higher spend.
lesson.l26.request.dark_mode_claim.hint: Try imagining the data broken out by device type alone - does the pattern survive?
lesson.l26.evidence.dark_mode_claim: Dark mode is only available on newer devices - the same devices whose owners already spend more, toggle or no toggle.
lesson.l26.option.dark_mode_claim.dark_m: Enabling dark mode is clearly boosting how much people spend
lesson.l26.option.dark_mode_claim.device: The device-group explanation doesn't actually rule anything out
Device type explains it - dark mode itself has nothing to do with spend
lesson.l26.explanation.dark_mode_claim.d: Once you control for device group, the relationship between dark mode and spend nearly disappears - that's not what a real driver of spend looks like.
The relationship vanishing once device group is held constant is exactly what ruling it out looks like.
Right - within the modern-device group alone, dark mode and spend barely correlate at all. Device type explains almost the whole pattern.
lesson.l26.twist_randomized_treatment_la: Randomized test: LTV with the program
lesson.l26.twist_randomized_control_labe: Randomized test: LTV without the program
lesson.l26.field.what_is_supported.promp: Across all three investigations, what's actually been established?
lesson.l26.field.what_is_supported.hint: Think about what a real, strong correlation can and can't tell you on its own.
lesson.l26.option.what_is_supported.dire: Direct causation, confirmed in every case
lesson.l26.option.what_is_supported.a_re: A real pattern, not a proven cause
lesson.l26.option.what_is_supported.stro: A correlation this strong is like an experiment
lesson.l26.field.next_evidence.prompt: What kind of evidence would actually help settle a case like this?
lesson.l26.field.next_evidence.hint: Think about what the loyalty program's real test looked like.
lesson.l26.option.next_evidence.a_bigger: A bigger sample of the same correlational data
lesson.l26.option.next_evidence.a_random: A randomized test, or ruling out the alternatives
dialogue.l26_briefing.line1: Push opens and weekly spend move together like this. Marketing wants to double down on notifications immediately.
dialogue.l26_briefing.line2: It's obviously the notifications driving it - look at that pattern.
dialogue.l26_briefing.line3: A real pattern doesn't prove why it's there. Let's check what else could explain the exact same numbers.
dialogue.l26_investigation.line1: Every one of these correlations is real - the question was never whether it exists, it's what's actually causing it.
dialogue.l26_investigation.line2: Direct causation, reverse causation, and a hidden third factor can all produce the exact same correlation.
dialogue.l26_investigation.line3: Pick the verdict you'd actually stand behind for each case.
dialogue.l26_independent_intro.line1: Same three cases, no hints this time.
dialogue.l26_twist.line1: NovaMart once saw a huge gap between loyalty members and everyone else, and spent big on the program because of it.
dialogue.l26_twist.line2: Here's what a real randomized test later found.
dialogue.l26_debrief.line1: So almost none of that gap was actually the program.
dialogue.l26_debrief.line2: Most of it was self-selection - the customers who'd already spend more were also the ones who signed up.
dialogue.l26_debrief.line3: That's exactly the trap all three of today's cases were built to catch.
lesson.l27.title: Causality Courtroom
lesson.l27.objective1: Recognize when a comparison group selected itself instead of being assigned
lesson.l27.objective2: Tell a real effect apart from who simply showed up in each group
lesson.l27.objective3: Deliver a verdict that states its own reasoning and limitations
lesson.l27.request.tool_spend_claim.prom: Exhibit A: customers who use the budgeting tool spend far less on impulse purchases. Counsel argues the tool is clearly working.
lesson.l27.request.tool_spend_claim.hint: Ask who actually ended up using the tool, and why.
lesson.l27.evidence.tool_spend_claim: Tool adoption was entirely opt-in - customers turned it on themselves, nobody was assigned to use it.
lesson.l27.option.tool_spend_claim.susta: Sustain - self-selection could fully explain this gap
lesson.l27.option.tool_spend_claim.overr: Overrule - a correlation this strong basically proves it works
lesson.l27.option.tool_spend_claim.susta: Sustain - the two groups aren't even the same size
Right - people who already spend carefully were the ones likely to turn the tool on. The tool's own real effect is still unknown.
A strong correlation doesn't rule out self-selection - the people who chose the tool may have already been the bigger savers.
Both groups are the same size here - and even if they weren't, that alone wouldn't be the actual problem with this comparison.
lesson.l27.request.resolution_satisfacti: Exhibit B: tickets resolved within an hour score far higher satisfaction. Counsel argues we should mandate 1-hour resolution everywhere.
Ask what actually determines whether a ticket can be resolved that fast.
lesson.l27.evidence.resolution_satisfact: Tickets resolved within an hour are overwhelmingly simple issues - complex ones structurally can't be resolved that fast, no matter the effort.
lesson.l27.option.resolution_satisfactio: Overrule - customers clearly reward speed, mandate it everywhere
Sustain - fast tickets are just the easy ones, not proof speed satisfies
Sustain - fast tickets probably go to your best agents
lesson.l27.explanation.resolution_satisf: Mandating speed doesn't make a hard ticket easy - it just guarantees rushed answers to problems that needed more time.
Right - ticket difficulty selects the resolution time here, not the other way around. Speed alone was never the driver.
The evidence points to ticket difficulty, not agent skill - a ticket is fast because it's simple, not because a stronger agent took it.
lesson.l27.request.training_performance_: Exhibit C: employees who completed the optional training scored 20% higher on reviews. Counsel argues the training clearly works.
Ask who actually bothered to sign up for an optional, barely-advertised program.
lesson.l27.evidence.training_performance: The training was entirely optional and mentioned in a single email - almost no one who wasn't already a strong performer signed up.
lesson.l27.option.training_performance_c: Overrule - a 20% gap is too large for coincidence, the training gets credit
Sustain - performance reviews are always biased regardless
Sustain - can't separate the training from who chose to attend
lesson.l27.explanation.training_performa: Being too large for coincidence isn't the same as being caused by the training - strong performers self-selecting in produces the exact same gap.
That objection would apply to every review ever given - it doesn't engage with what's actually wrong with this specific comparison.
Right - an optional, barely-advertised program mostly reaches people who were already ahead. The training's own effect is still unmeasured.
lesson.l27.twist_randomized_treatment_la: Randomized test: conversion with new checkout
lesson.l27.twist_randomized_control_labe: Randomized test: conversion with old checkout
lesson.l27.field.final_verdict.prompt: What's the responsible verdict across all three cases?
lesson.l27.field.final_verdict.hint: Think about what every one of these comparisons actually has in common.
lesson.l27.option.final_verdict.all_conf: Confirmed - effects too large for chance
lesson.l27.option.final_verdict.each_nee: Each needs a proper comparison group
lesson.l27.option.final_verdict.all_shou: Throw out all three claims entirely
lesson.l27.field.missing_evidence.prompt: What would actually settle whether these effects are real?
lesson.l27.field.missing_evidence.hint: Think about what the checkout beta's real test looked like.
lesson.l27.option.missing_evidence.more_: A bigger sample of the same data
dialogue.l27_briefing.line1: Three teams brought me claims this week, all backed by strong-looking numbers, all asking for budget.
dialogue.l27_briefing.line2: I need someone to actually cross-examine these before I sign off.
dialogue.l27_briefing.line3: Then let's treat each one like a case - the numbers might be real, but that doesn't mean the story attached to them is.
dialogue.l27_investigation.line1: Every one of these correlations is real - nobody's making up the numbers.
dialogue.l27_investigation.line2: The question is who ended up in each group, and whether that alone explains the gap.
dialogue.l27_investigation.line3: Sustain the objection if the comparison doesn't hold up. Overrule it if it does.
dialogue.l27_independent_intro.line1: Same three cases, no hints this time.
dialogue.l27_twist.line1: NovaMart once had an opt-in checkout beta that looked like a massive win.
dialogue.l27_twist.line2: Here's what a real randomized test found once nobody could self-select anymore.
dialogue.l27_debrief.line1: So the real effect was a fraction of what the beta numbers suggested.
dialogue.l27_debrief.line2: Every case today had the same shape - a real gap, and a group that got there on its own.
dialogue.l27_debrief.line3: A verdict without a proper comparison group is just a good story wearing a number.
lesson.l28.title: Chart Crime Lab
lesson.l28.objective1: Recognize when a chart's axis, window, or denominator is doing the persuading
lesson.l28.objective2: Redraw a chart so its visual impression matches its real numbers
lesson.l28.objective3: Approve, reject, or redesign a chart and explain why
lesson.l28.request.satisfaction_score_cl: Customer satisfaction rose from 72 to 75 this year. Leadership wants a chart that makes the improvement land.
A real 3-point gain can be drawn to look like almost anything, depending on where the axis starts.
lesson.l28.request.active_users_claim.pr: Someone wants a chart of monthly active users for the year-end deck.
lesson.l28.request.active_users_claim.hi: Check what the months you're not showing actually did.
lesson.l28.request.returns_rate_claim.pr: The ops team wants a chart of the product return rate by quarter.
lesson.l28.request.returns_rate_claim.hi: Ask what a return rate should actually be measured against.
lesson.l28.twist_spend_change_label: Marketing spend, change over the year
lesson.l28.field.chart_review_standard.p: What's the right standard for approving a chart before it goes out?
lesson.l28.field.chart_review_standard.h: Think about what made the dual-axis chart misleading despite correct numbers.
Numbers and visuals both must be honest
Only the written report needs to be accurate
lesson.l28.field.general_lesson.prompt: What's the general lesson from today?
lesson.l28.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what stayed the same across every flawed chart today.
lesson.l28.option.general_lesson.same_da: The same data looks different sliced
lesson.l28.option.general_lesson.dual_ax: Dual-axis charts are always the right choice
dialogue.l28_briefing.line1: Marketing keeps sending me charts to double-check before they go out, and something feels off about a few of them.
dialogue.l28_briefing.line2: The numbers all check out - it's something about how they're drawn.
dialogue.l28_briefing.line3: That's the actual crime scene here. A chart can be completely honest about its numbers and still mislead everyone who looks at it.
dialogue.l28_investigation.line1: Same real data every time - only how it's scaled, windowed, or divided changes.
dialogue.l28_investigation.line2: A truncated axis, a cherry-picked date range, and the wrong denominator all do the same job: make a real number tell a different story.
dialogue.l28_investigation.line3: Pick the version you'd actually publish.
dialogue.l28_independent_intro.line1: Same three charts, no hints this time.
dialogue.l28_twist.line1: NovaMart's growth team once put spend and sign-ups on a dual-axis chart, scaled so the two lines matched almost exactly.
dialogue.l28_twist.line2: Here's what the same two numbers actually did, in their own terms.
dialogue.l28_debrief.line1: So the dual-axis chart wasn't wrong about a single number.
dialogue.l28_debrief.line2: It didn't have to be. Choosing the scale was the whole trick.
dialogue.l28_debrief.line3: A chart earns approval by being honest twice - once in its numbers, once in how it shows them.
lesson.l29.title: The Executive Brief
lesson.l29.objective1: Tell a decision-relevant finding apart from a merely dramatic one
lesson.l29.objective2: Select findings, evidence, and a recommendation that actually fit together
lesson.l29.objective3: Deliver a brief that's accurate, useful, and appropriately cautious
lesson.l29.picker_prompt: The board asked one question: is the checkout redesign working? Pick the three findings that actually answer it.
lesson.l29.picker_hint: A number moving a lot doesn't mean it moved because of the redesign.
lesson.l29.twist_title: The Number That Made the Brief
lesson.l29.finding.checkout_completion: Checkout completion rate rose from 68% to 72%, holding steady for six weeks.
lesson.l29.finding.payment_step_abandonm: Cart abandonment at the payment step dropped from 22% to 17%.
lesson.l29.finding.order_value_and_retur: Average order value and return rate both held steady.
lesson.l29.finding.social_mentions: Social media mentions of NovaMart spiked 300% this month.
lesson.l29.finding.stock_price: NovaMart's stock price rose 9% this month.

lesson.l29.finding.support_tickets_confu: Support tickets mentioning a confusing checkout dropped 60%.

lesson.l29.field.supporting_chart.hint: Pick the chart that shows the finding actually driving the recommendation.
lesson.l29.field.confidence_level.prompt: How confident should the brief be?

lesson.l29.option.confidence_level.very_: Very high - proves the redesign was a triumph
lesson.l29.option.confidence_level.high_: High - sustained six weeks, clear mechanism
lesson.l29.option.confidence_level.low_c: Low - could easily be random noise
lesson.l29.field.recommendation.hint: Think about what the evidence supports, not just what feels safest.
lesson.l29.option.recommendation.revert_: Revert to the old checkout immediately
lesson.l29.option.recommendation.keep_an: Keep the new checkout, watch the return rate
lesson.l29.field.caveats.prompt: What caveat does the brief most need?
lesson.l29.field.caveats.hint: Think about what else changed the same month that could blur the story.
lesson.l29.option.caveats.sample_size_wa: The sample size was only ten customers
lesson.l29.option.caveats.competitor_red: A rival also redesigned checkout that month
lesson.l29.option.caveats.leadership_mig: Leadership might not like this result

dialogue.l29_briefing.line1: The board wants three minutes on the checkout redesign, not thirty slides. Give me the brief.
dialogue.l29_briefing.line2: We've got dozens of numbers from this quarter - pick the ones that actually matter.
dialogue.l29_briefing.line3: Dozens of real numbers doesn't mean dozens of good reasons. Let's find the three that actually answer the question.
dialogue.l29_investigation.line1: Every number in this pool is real. The question isn't which ones are true, it's which ones are actually about the redesign.
dialogue.l29_investigation.line2: A dramatic number and a decision-relevant number are not always the same number.
dialogue.l29_investigation.line3: Pick the three findings you'd actually put in front of the board.
dialogue.l29_independent_intro.line1: Same pool, no hints this time.
dialogue.l29_twist.line1: Marketing once led a brief with 'app downloads spiked 500% this week' to justify a UI investment.
dialogue.l29_twist.line2: Here's the metric that actually mattered for the UI change - the one that never made the brief.
dialogue.l29_debrief.line1: So the flashiest number in the room isn't automatically the one that matters.
dialogue.l29_debrief.line2: It rarely is. A dramatic number gets attention. A decision-relevant one earns it.
dialogue.l29_debrief.line3: The brief you just wrote says exactly as much as the evidence supports, and not one word more.
lesson.l30.title: The Data Incident
lesson.l30.objective1: Decide which investigations are worth running, and read their evidence honestly
lesson.l30.objective2: Recognize when an intuitive first explanation is incomplete
lesson.l30.objective3: Communicate root-cause confidence, business impact, and next steps in one report
dialogue.l30_briefing.line1: Revenue just dropped 18% week over week. Everyone's waiting on an explanation.
dialogue.l30_briefing.line2: Whatever it is, I need real numbers before this goes anywhere near leadership.
dialogue.l30_briefing.line3: My money's on the checkout redesign. It shipped right before this happened.
dialogue.l30_briefing.line4: Maybe. Let's not assume anything yet - let's go find out.

dialogue.l30_investigation_intro.line2: Some of what you find will matter. Some of it won't. That's the job.
dialogue.l30_debrief.line1: That's the real story - and it's less dramatic than it looked this morning.
dialogue.l30_debrief.line2: Good. That was one step from an email to the whole company about a 'checkout crisis.'
dialogue.l30_debrief.line3: Get the dashboard fixed so this doesn't happen again next quarter.
dialogue.l30_debrief.line4: Regional monitoring, not just the company-wide total. Filing the ticket now.
lesson.l30.hub_prompt: Choose where to look. Investigate at least three leads, then conclude the investigation.
lesson.l30.lead_label.regional_breakdown: Break the drop down by region
lesson.l30.lead.redesign_correlation.pro: Some people are already blaming the checkout redesign that shipped company-wide 10 days ago. Does the evidence support that?
lesson.l30.lead.redesign_correlation.hin: If the redesign broke checkout, regions with a bigger revenue drop should also show more support tickets - not fewer.
lesson.l30.evidence.redesign_correlation: The redesign shipped in every region on the exact same day.
lesson.l30.option.redesign_correlation.r: This confirms the redesign broke checkout

handbook.article.asking_an_analytical_qu: A stakeholder asks a question that sounds perfectly clear until you try to answer it. "Are customers becoming less loyal?" has an obvious-sounding yes-or-no shape, but nothing about the sentence says which customers, over what period, based on what behavior, or what "loyal" is even supposed to mean. That gap, between a question that sounds answerable and a question a dataset can actually answer, is where a surprising amount of bad analysis starts - not in the numbers themselves.

The reason a vague question survives this long is that it doesn't feel vague from the inside. "Less loyal" already conjures a specific mental picture for whoever asked it - probably repeat purchases, or maybe app opens, or maybe just a gut sense that something's off. The trouble is that everyone who hears the question fills in their own picture, and two people can walk away agreeing to "check if customers are less loyal" while meaning two different measurable things. An analytical question is one where that filling-in has already happened on paper: who's being counted, over what window, based on what specific behavior, and against what earlier baseline.

Turning a vague ask into an analytical one usually means pinning down the same handful of things every time: which unit you're actually counting (an order? a customer? a session?), over what stretch of time, within which slice of the population, against which specific metric, and - easy to forget - what decision the answer is actually going to inform. That last one matters more than it looks: a number can be perfectly correct and still useless if nobody can say what changes depending on whether it comes back high or low.

Being this specific has a real cost, and it's worth naming rather than pretending precision is free. A question pinned down too early can blind you to the thing actually worth finding: if "loyal" gets defined as "made a second purchase within 30 days" before anyone's looked at the data, a genuinely different and more interesting pattern (say, a huge drop specifically among customers who contacted support) can sail right past unnoticed, because nobody was looking for it. The fix isn't to stay vague; it's to treat the first specific version of the question as a working draft, not a locked contract, specific enough to start analyzing and loose enough to revise once the data actually starts talking back.

None of this guarantees the question is the right one to be asking in the first place. A perfectly well-specified brief can still measure something that doesn't actually matter to the business, or answer a narrower version of the real concern behind it. Sharpening a question makes it operationalized and answerable with data; it doesn't make it wise. That judgment (is this even the question worth spending the week on) stays a human call no amount of structure replaces.
handbook.article.observation_unit_and_gr: Two questions shape a dataset more than most people realize, and both get skipped more often than they should: what, exactly, does one row represent, and at what level of detail was it recorded? The first is what this course calls the observation unit; the second is the grain. In practice the two ideas often overlap, and the sharp line drawn between them here is a teaching simplification, not a strict rule the rest of the industry follows. Neither shows up as a labeled column anywhere - they're properties of the table as a whole, and getting them wrong doesn't usually throw an error. It just quietly produces a number that means something other than what everyone assumes it means.

The observation unit is the thing you're counting - the unit you'd point to and say "that's one." An order is one thing; a customer is another; a single line item inside an order is a third, even though all three might live in tables that look superficially similar. NovaMart's own analytical brief makes this an explicit, unavoidable first choice for exactly this reason: before anyone can argue about whether a number is high or low, everyone answering the question has to be counting the same kind of thing.

Grain is the related but separate question of how fine or coarse that counting actually is - whether a row represents one order, one order line, one customer-day, or one customer-month. A revenue table can honestly claim to be "per order" and still hide a real problem if what's actually needed is "per order line," because a single order with three products would already be summed into one number before anyone gets a chance to look at the products separately.

Grain mismatches are dangerous specifically because they don't announce themselves. Summing a column that's actually recorded at a finer grain than you think produces a real number, one that runs without complaint through every downstream calculation - it's just the wrong number, inflated or deflated by however many extra rows each real-world entity happened to contribute. The fix isn't a special check for this one failure mode; it's asking, before writing a single line of aggregation code, "what does one row in this table actually represent" and confirming the answer out loud rather than assuming it matches whatever the column names suggest.

Choosing a grain is also a real trade-off, not just a fact to get right. Finer-grained data often makes it possible to build a coarser view later, as long as the dimensions and raw measures that view will need were actually kept and the aggregation itself is done correctly - simply summing values that are already averages, rates, or unique counts produces a wrong number, not just a less detailed one. Finer data is also heavier to store, slower to query, and easier to draw a wrong conclusion from if someone aggregates it incorrectly. Coarser data is lighter and faster, but it locks in a specific view of the world at collection time.

That limit plays out differently depending on what's actually being aggregated. Revenue is additive, so a table stored "per day" sums correctly into "per month": each day's total is a real piece of the month's total. A daily conversion rate is different: a simple average of daily conversion rates is not generally the true multi-day rate, because days rarely have the same number of eligible sessions, and an unweighted average silently treats them as if they did. It's still possible to recompute the rate correctly at a coarser grain without ever touching raw events, as long as its two components (conversions and eligible sessions) were both kept and summed on their own - dividing the summed conversions by the summed eligible sessions gives the true multi-day rate, equivalent to weighting each day's rate by that day's own session count rather than averaging the percentages directly. The rate itself doesn't need to be additive if what it's built from is. Daily unique users is the harder case. Knowing 500 people were active Monday and 500 Tuesday says nothing about whether they were the same 500 or 1,000 different ones, and no amount of correctly-kept daily counts can answer that; a real monthly figure needs the underlying identity information, not just more detailed sums. When there's real doubt about what a future question might need, the safer default is keeping data finer, and keeping the specific components a rate is built from rather than just the rate itself.
handbook.article.metrics_need_definition: Two teams can each pull "active users" for the exact same week, using the exact same underlying event log, and walk away with two different numbers - and neither team made a mistake. "Active" sounds like a fact about a user until you notice it was never actually specified: active by opening the app once? By completing an action? Within the last day, the last 7, the last 30? Every one of those is a defensible reading of the word, and every one produces a different count from the same raw data.

This isn't a data-quality problem in the usual sense - the events themselves can be perfectly clean and complete. The gap lives entirely in the metric's own definition, or lack of one. A metric name is a promise to measure something specific; until someone writes down exactly which action, over exactly which window, counted exactly how (once per user? once per session? every occurrence?), the name is doing more work than the definition actually supports.

Tightening a loose definition always trades away something. A stricter "active" (say, completing a specific in-app action rather than merely opening it) excludes behavior that a looser definition would have counted, and that's not a flaw to apologize for: it's the price of the number meaning the same thing to everyone who reads it. Which definition is "right" isn't something the data can settle by itself - it depends on which construct the number is actually meant to represent. The alternative, leaving "active" comfortably vague, keeps every reader free to imagine their own favorable interpretation, which is a worse trade the moment the number has to justify a real decision rather than just describe a vague trend.

A written-down definition isn't a permanent fix, either. It has a shelf life tied to whatever the product actually does: the moment NovaMart ships a feature that changes what "using the app" even means - a new passive notification that technically opens a session without anyone touching anything, say - yesterday's careful definition of "active" can start quietly measuring the wrong thing again, precisely because nobody thought to revisit it. A metric definition is something to maintain, not something to write once and trust forever.
handbook.article.time_windows_change_ans: The same NovaMart metric, pulled the same afternoon by the same person, can show a 4-point improvement or a 2-point decline depending on nothing but which stretch of time it's measured against. Both computations can be arithmetically correct; they don't have to be equally appropriate answers to the actual question being asked. Two different, unstated questions happened to get asked using the same words.

An analytical brief's timeframe field forces one specific window into the open for a single question - this metric, this period, full stop. The broader pattern this article is actually about is what happens across many questions: any time a result is compared against "before," the choice of how far back "before" reaches is doing real, silent work on the answer, whether or not anyone wrote it down as a formal timeframe.

A short window is responsive - it reflects a recent change quickly - but it's also noisy, prone to making an ordinary bad week look like a trend and an ordinary good week look like a breakthrough. A long window smooths that noise out, but it's slow to notice a real, recent shift, and it can bury a genuine two-week problem inside twelve months of otherwise-fine numbers.

Neither length is generically correct; the right one depends on what the number is actually for. A metric feeding a same-day operational alert needs a short window almost by definition - waiting a quarter to confirm a real outage defeats the point of alerting at all. A metric feeding an annual strategic decision needs enough history to separate a real shift from ordinary week-to-week noise, and a short window there risks reacting to something that would have resolved itself by next month.

Even a well-chosen window doesn't settle the question by itself, and a window shouldn't be picked only after seeing which one produces the preferred answer - that's cherry-picking a result, not choosing a methodology. Two honestly-chosen windows can still disagree, and when they do, the disagreement itself is information: it can point to real seasonality, an underlying trend, a genuine shift in conditions, or a baseline that's moved - not necessarily to one window being secretly the "real" one and the other wrong. Always state which window a number came from, and treat any switch between windows as a methodological decision that needs a real justification, not a silent default.
handbook.article.schema_is_a_contract.bo: A shipment record in NovaMart's fulfillment export carries a column called shipment_id, and every value in it is a plain integer: 100042, 100043, and so on. Nothing about that column's dtype raises a flag - int64 is exactly what a well-behaved numeric column looks like. And yet running shipment_id.mean() is perfectly legal code that answers a question nobody asked. The number it produces is real and computable, and completely meaningless, because shipment_id was never a quantity to begin with. It's a label wearing a number's clothing.

That's the gap between a column's physical representation and its semantic type, and a dtype only ever answers the first question. Sometimes pandas infers that dtype from the raw bytes; sometimes a loader is told it explicitly - dtype=, parse_dates=, a declared schema - so a column's physical type can be a deliberate choice, not just a guess. Neither path touches the second question. A semantic type is a much larger, open-ended judgment: identifier, timestamp, currency, duration, category, a genuine measurement. Whether a number is a quantity or a label is a fact about the business behind the data, not about how carefully its bytes were typed.

The more dangerous version of this gap doesn't even announce itself with a wrong-looking dtype. A column can already be exactly the type it should be, a clean float64, and still be wrong, because the unit or convention behind those numbers quietly changed for part of the data. Picture a delivery-duration column that switches from minutes to seconds for one source system after an unflagged migration: no parse error, no missing value, every row still a valid number. The computation runs, returns a plausible-looking figure, and measures the wrong thing for however many rows came from that one source - a failure a dtype check will never catch, because there's nothing in it for a dtype check to catch.

What actually resolves both cases is the same thing: a data contract, an explicit statement of what a column means, what unit or format it's in, and which operations on it are legitimate - going beyond anything a dtype alone can express. A contract isn't something a dataset carries automatically. It's an agreement between whoever produces a column and whoever consumes it, and like any agreement between two systems, it can go stale the moment one side changes without telling the other. A new source system, a redefined field, a migration nobody thought to flag in the analysis itself - none of these need to touch a single dtype to break the contract underneath it.

None of this makes df.dtypes useless. It's still the fastest way to spot the columns that are obviously wrong: identifiers stored with stray punctuation, dates still sitting in a string column. What it can't do is vouch for a column that already shows the "right" dtype, because rightness at that level was never the question a contract actually answers. Ask a second question of every column that matters to the result, every time: not just what type is this, but what is it supposed to mean, and does what actually arrived still match that.
handbook.glossary.analytical_question.de: A business question rewritten precisely enough to check against data: which unit is being counted, over what timeframe, within which population, against which specific metric, and for what decision. A vague question ("are customers less loyal?") can sound answerable while actually meaning several different measurable things at once. See "Asking an Analytical Question" for the trade-offs involved in getting this specific.
handbook.glossary.observation_unit.defin: The specific thing a dataset counts one row of - an order, a customer, a single line item - even when several of these look similar at a glance. Getting this wrong doesn't crash anything; it just means two people can compute a "correct" number about two different kinds of things without noticing.
handbook.glossary.grain.definition: How fine or coarse a dataset's own rows are recorded: a table can track a customer overall, a customer per day, or a customer per product per day - each a valid but different grain for describing "the same" customer. In practice, observation unit and grain often overlap; this course's sharp distinction between them is a teaching simplification, not a strict industry-wide rule. Also seen called "granularity" outside this course.
handbook.glossary.metric_definition.defi: The exact, written-down rule behind a metric's name: which action counts, over what window, counted how many times per user. A metric name alone ("active users") is a promise a definition has to actually keep - without one, two teams computing "the same" metric can honestly disagree.
handbook.glossary.time_window.definition: The span of time a result is actually computed or compared over - last 7 days, last quarter, year over year. The same metric can show improvement or decline depending only on which window it's read through; both readings can be arithmetically correct without being equally appropriate answers to the question being asked. Distinct, in this course's own terminology, from Timeframe - the specific brief field naming one fixed window for a single analytical question. In everyday use the two words are often interchangeable; the distinction here is a deliberate teaching convention, not a universal rule.
handbook.glossary.timeframe.definition: The specific time period named in an analytical brief for one particular question - a fixed input, not a general concept. See Time Window for the broader idea that different window choices can change a result even outside a formal brief. This course draws a deliberate line between the two terms as a teaching convention; general usage doesn't always keep them this separate.
handbook.glossary.population.definition: The full group a question is actually about, before any sampling or filtering happens - all NovaMart customers, or specifically all customers in one market. Naming the population precisely matters as much as naming the metric: a true statement about one slice can be silently misread as a claim about everyone.
handbook.glossary.sample.definition: A subset of a population actually examined, used to say something about the whole without checking every member. How that subset gets chosen (see Sampling) determines whether conclusions drawn from it can honestly generalize back to the full population.
handbook.glossary.sampling.definition: The method used to choose which members of a population end up in a sample. A biased method - even one applied perfectly consistently - can produce a sample that looks representative and isn't. This course's own Sampling Mission lesson explores exactly this problem in depth.
handbook.glossary.confounder.definition: A third factor that influences both sides of an apparent relationship, making two things look connected when the real cause is something else entirely. A real correlation can be completely genuine and still not mean what it first appears to, once a confounder is accounted for.
